title: Sources of sound: shaking, blowing, popping and rubbing

summary.text: Tap a glass bottle that has water in it, and more water gives a lower note. Blow across the same bottle, and more water gives a higher note. Same bottle, same water, opposite order. Your child finds out why, by asking what actually shakes in each case. Then comes the sound of a damp finger squeaking on glass, a clap that has no steady note, and a whispered 'ee' and 'oo' that can still be told apart with no buzz in the throat at all. Every sound starts with air being pushed, but there are four different ways to push it. A note belongs partly to what makes it and partly to the space that shapes it. Nobody yet knows exactly why some pairs of notes sound sweet to nearly everyone.
summary.art: A row of glass bottles with different amounts of water on a kitchen table, a spoon tapping one, a child blowing across another, and a damp finger squeaking on a window.

intro.hook: Line up three glass bottles with different amounts of water. Tap each one with a spoon and listen. The fullest bottle gives the lowest note. Now blow gently across the top of each bottle, like blowing across a flute. Listen again. Is the fullest bottle still the lowest?
intro.text: It is not. The order flips over. The same bottle makes a low note when you tap it and a high note when you blow across it. In this unit you find out what shakes in each case, and why that matters. You also meet three other ways to make a sound, by popping, by rubbing and by whispering, and you test them with things from your kitchen and your window.
intro.art: Three glass bottles with different water levels, a spoon tapping one and a child blowing across the mouth of another.

outcomes: I can name four different ways a sound can start: a solid thing shaking, air shaking in a space, a sudden pop and rubbing that sticks and slips.
I can explain that pitch is counted in hertz, the number of vibrations each second, and that halving the length of a string or a pipe makes the note an octave higher.
I can explain why a plucked string sounds like one note but really holds many, and what overtones and timbre are.
I can test with bottles how tapping and blowing give opposite orders of notes, and explain it by what is shaking.
I can explain how wind or breath across an edge makes a whistle, a flute note or the hum of a wire.
I can explain that a pop is a sudden push of air, and that a squeak comes from a surface that sticks and slips again and again.
I can explain that a voice is a buzz from the vocal folds, shaped by the throat and mouth, and show that vowels are made by the shaping.
I can say what scientists still argue about, such as why some notes sound sweet together.

terms.meaning: The unit for counting vibrations. One hertz is one vibration each second. It is written Hz. A note of 440 hertz vibrates 440 times each second.
terms.example: A child's speaking voice is often between 250 and 400 hertz. A grown-up man's is often about 100 to 120 hertz.
terms.art: A stopwatch showing one second beside a tuning fork, with 440 tiny wavy lines drawn inside the second.

terms.meaning: The gap between a note and the note that vibrates exactly twice as fast. The two notes sound like the same note, one low and one high.
terms.example: In Indian music, the Sa in the middle and the upper Sa are one octave apart.
terms.art: Two strings on a stand, one of them exactly half the length of the other, with two matching notes drawn above them.

terms.meaning: The lowest and usually the strongest vibration in a sound. It sets the pitch that you hear.
terms.example: When you pluck a string, the vibration of the whole string is the fundamental.
terms.art: A plucked string vibrating as one single long loop.

terms.meaning: A higher vibration that sounds at the same time as the fundamental. A string vibrates in halves, thirds and quarters at once, and each way makes an overtone.
terms.example: A plucked string rings with its fundamental and with overtones above it, but you hear them all as one note.
terms.art: A string drawn four times: one loop, two loops, three loops and four loops, all stacked on top of each other.

terms.meaning: The quality of a sound, which tells a flute from a violin even when both play the same note. It comes from which overtones are strong and which are weak. Say it TAM-ber.
terms.example: A bansuri and a veena can play the same note, and you can still tell which is which.
terms.art: A flute and a veena playing the same note, with two different bar charts of overtones beside them.

terms.meaning: When something vibrates strongly because the vibration it is given matches its own natural pitch. Air in a bottle has resonance at some pitches and not at others.
terms.example: Sing slowly up a scale near the mouth of an empty bottle. At one note, the bottle suddenly booms.
terms.art: A child singing at the mouth of a bottle, with the bottle glowing and shaking at one note.

terms.meaning: The air inside a pipe, bottle or tube, as a standing column of air. A longer air column gives a lower note. A shorter one gives a higher note.
terms.example: In a bottle with water in it, the air column is the part from the water to the top.
terms.art: A bottle cut open to show the water at the bottom and a labelled column of air above it.

terms.meaning: A tone made when a stream of air hits a sharp edge. The air swirls to one side, then the other, and each swirl pushes the air around it.
terms.example: A whistle, a bansuri and a bottle you blow across all make edge tones.
terms.art: A thin stream of air from lips hitting the sharp edge of a bottle's mouth, with small swirls drawn on either side.

terms.meaning: A spinning swirl in air or water, like the little whirl behind a spoon moved through tea.
terms.example: When wind blows past a wire, it forms vortexes behind the wire, and the wire can hum.
terms.art: A wire in a wind, with a line of small spinning swirls trailing behind it.

terms.meaning: Two surfaces that rub, grip, then slip, then grip again, many times each second. It makes a squeak or a screech.
terms.example: A damp finger moved across a window sticks and slips, and squeaks.
terms.art: A finger on a window with tiny arrows showing it gripping and slipping in tiny jumps.

terms.meaning: A short, sudden push in the air that spreads out. A pop or a clap is one pressure pulse, not a long steady vibration.
terms.example: A balloon bursting makes a pressure pulse that you hear as a bang.
terms.art: A balloon bursting, with one ring of squeezed air spreading outwards.

terms.meaning: A very strong pressure pulse that moves faster than sound. It is heard as a crack or a boom.
terms.example: Thunder is a shock wave from the sudden heating of the air by lightning.
terms.art: A lightning bolt in the sky with a bright ring of squeezed air spreading from it.

terms.meaning: The space above your vocal folds: the throat, the mouth and the nose. It shapes the buzz from your vocal folds into the sounds of speech.
terms.example: When you change your mouth from 'ee' to 'oo', you change the shape of your vocal tract.
terms.art: A side view of a head with the throat, mouth and nose space shaded.

terms.meaning: A speech sound made with the mouth open, like 'ee', 'aa' or 'oo'. Each vowel has its own mouth shape, and the shape decides which overtones are strong.
terms.example: Sing one note and change the mouth from 'ee' to 'oo'. The note stays the same and the vowel changes.
terms.art: Three mouth shapes drawn side by side, wide for 'ee', open for 'aa' and round for 'oo'.

terms.meaning: A line on a vibrating plate or skin that stays still while the parts on either side move. Sand sprinkled on the plate collects along these lines.
terms.example: Sand on a steel plate that is rung with a violin bow gathers into lines and shapes.
terms.art: A square plate with sand collected in a star-shaped pattern of lines, and a violin bow at the edge.

terms.meaning: A sound that mixes many pitches with no steady note. A hiss, a clap and the crash of waves are noise.
terms.example: Air blown out of a tyre makes a hiss. A tuning fork makes a pure note.
terms.art: A pure note drawn as one smooth wave, beside a noise drawn as a jumble of many different wiggly lines.

explanations.concept: Four ways to start a sound
explanations.definition: A sound starts when something pushes on the air. There are four common ways: a solid thing shakes, air shakes inside a space, the air gets a sudden push, or two surfaces rub, stick and slip.
explanations.description: In the earlier unit you learned that every sound comes from something vibrating. That is true, and it is the most important idea. But it hides some differences. A shaking solid thing is the first way. A string, a drum skin, a bell, a steel plate or your vocal folds all push the air as they move. The second way is air shaking in a space. In a bansuri, a bottle or a conch, a stream of air or a tap sets the air inside shaking, and the shape of the space decides the note. The third way is a sudden push. A clap, a balloon bursting, a firecracker and thunder do not vibrate steadily. They squeeze the air once, hard, and the squeeze spreads out as a pop. The fourth way is rubbing. A damp finger on glass, chalk on a board, a squeaky door hinge and a cricket's wing all rub two surfaces together. They grip, slip, grip and slip again, hundreds or thousands of times each second, and that is a vibration too. In every case, something pushes on the air in a pattern, and the air carries the pattern to your ear. The four ways are not four different kinds of sound. They are four different ways to give the air a push. Real instruments often mix them. A bansuri uses air shaking in a space, and the player's breath also makes a hiss.
examples: A sitar string is a shaking solid. A bansuri is air shaking in a space. A clap is a sudden push. A squeaky chair is stick-slip.
A cricket rubs a rough edge on one wing across a row of ridges on the other, like running a stick along a comb.
A violin mixes the first and fourth ways. The bow sticks and slips on the string, and the string shakes.
explanations.art: Four panels: a string being plucked, a bottle being blown across, a balloon bursting, and a damp finger squeaking on glass, each with small arrows showing the push on the air.
explanations.context: This card gives the big picture of the unit: four different ways a sound can start. Each of the next cards takes one way and looks closely at it.

explanations.definition: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds. We count it in hertz, which is the number of vibrations each second. A higher pitch means more vibrations each second.
explanations.description: A string sounds high when it vibrates fast and low when it vibrates slowly. We can count how fast. One vibration each second is one hertz, written 1 Hz. The unit is named after Heinrich Hertz, a German scientist who first made radio waves in a lab in the 1880s. People can hear from about 20 hertz to about 20,000 hertz. The A that orchestras tune to is 440 hertz, which means a string or a column of air shakes 440 times every second. Voices are slower than that. A grown-up man's speaking voice is often about 100 to 120 hertz, a grown-up woman's about 200, and a child's about 250 to 400. The vocal folds open and close that many times each second. A honeybee's wings beat about 230 times each second, which makes her buzz. A mosquito's wings beat roughly 400 times or more each second, and that is why a mosquito whines higher than a bee. These numbers are too fast to count by eye. In the 1630s, a French priest and scientist, Marin Mersenne, found a way. He stretched a very long string until it vibrated slowly enough to count. He found rules for how the count changes with length, and used the rules to work out how fast short strings shake. It was one of the first times anyone counted a sound.
examples: A singer's Sa may be about 130 hertz for a man and about 260 hertz for a woman, and the tanpura is tuned to match it.
A mosquito whines near your ear because her wings beat several hundred times each second. A slower beat would sound like a buzz or a hum.
At 20 hertz, a sound is a rumble that you feel as much as hear. At 15,000 hertz, it is a thin hiss that many grown-ups can no longer hear.
explanations.art: A number line from 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz with small pictures at the right places: an elephant rumble, a man's voice, a child's voice, a mosquito, and a high squeak.
explanations.context: In the earlier unit you learned that a faster vibration gives a higher note. This card shows how scientists count that speed, and gives the numbers for things you know.

explanations.concept: Shorter means higher, in exact ratios
explanations.definition: If you halve the length of a string or of an air column, the note goes up by one octave, which is twice as many vibrations each second. Simple ratios of length give the notes that blend best.
explanations.description: Take a stretched string that gives the note Sa. Press it at its middle, so that only half of it can shake. It now vibrates twice as fast and gives the Sa one octave higher. A string two thirds as long vibrates one and a half times as fast and gives Pa. Sa and Pa are called a fifth in the Western system, and in Indian music theory they are samvadi, notes that agree. This is why the tanpura is tuned to Pa and Sa. The same rule works for pipes. The air in a pipe that is closed at one end vibrates at about the speed of sound divided by four times the pipe's length. Sound moves about 343 metres each second in warm air. So a closed pipe 17 centimetres long gives about 500 hertz, and one 34 centimetres long gives about 250 hertz, which is one octave lower. The rule for strings was written down by Mersenne in 1636. The rules say that vibration speed goes up when the string is shorter, tighter or thinner. It goes down when the string is longer, looser or thicker. There was an old story that Pythagoras found the ratios by listening to a blacksmith's hammers of different weights. Galileo pointed out in 1638 that the story cannot be true, because hammers of those weights do not give those notes. The ratios were real. How they were found is a legend.
examples: A veena has frets that shorten the string. Stopping it halfway gives the octave above the open string.
A bansuri hole near the end gives a high note, because the air column is short. All the holes covered gives the lowest note.
If a closed bottle air column is 20 centimetres long and another is 10 centimetres, the 10 centimetre one gives a note an octave higher.
explanations.art: Three strings of the same material, one full length, one half length and one two thirds length, with note names Sa, upper Sa and Pa beside them.
explanations.context: Why does a shorter string sound higher, and by how much? This card gives the exact rule, and shows how it works for strings and for air columns.

explanations.concept: A note is many notes: overtones and timbre
explanations.definition: A plucked string or a played pipe vibrates in many ways at once. The slowest is the fundamental, and the faster ones are overtones. The mix of overtones gives a sound its timbre.
explanations.description: Pluck a string and it seems to make one note. But the string does not only swing as one big loop. It also swings in two halves, in three thirds, in four quarters and more, all at the same moment. Each way of swinging makes its own tone. The slowest is the fundamental, and it sets the pitch you hear. The faster ones are overtones, and they are quieter. In 1636 Marin Mersenne was the first to report that he could hear the higher tones ringing above a plucked string. Your ear and brain mix them into one note. How strong each overtone is changes the character of the sound. This is called timbre. A flute has few strong overtones and sounds smooth. A sitar has many and sounds rich and buzzy. The tanpura has a special curved bridge, with a thread slipped under each string. The string brushes against the bridge as it swings, and this adds many strong overtones. The Indian scientist C. V. Raman studied this in the 1920s, and it gives the tanpura its shimmering sound. In 1822 the French mathematician Joseph Fourier showed that any repeating wave can be built from simple waves added together. In 1863 the German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz used this to show that timbre is the mix of overtones. Plates and skins have overtones too. In 1787 the German physicist Ernst Chladni bowed a metal plate with sand on it. The sand jumped away from the parts that shook and gathered along lines that stayed still. Each note gave a different pattern. Napoleon saw this, and the French Academy offered a prize for a mathematical explanation. The self-taught mathematician Sophie Germain entered three times and won in 1816.
examples: A bansuri and a violin can play the same Sa, and you can still tell them apart. Their overtones are different.
Touch a string lightly at its middle and pluck it. You hear a note one octave higher with a pure, bell-like sound, because the touch stops the fundamental and leaves the second overtone.
Sand on a bowed plate gathers into star-like patterns. Each pattern shows one way the plate can vibrate.
explanations.art: A plucked string drawn in four rows showing one, two, three and four loops, and a bar chart on the right showing how strong each is for two instruments.
explanations.context: Two instruments can play the same note and still sound different. This card explains why, with overtones and timbre.

explanations.concept: Air in a bottle: why tapping and blowing give opposite orders
explanations.definition: When you tap a bottle, the glass and the water shake. When you blow across it, the air inside shakes. More water makes the first note lower and the second note higher.
explanations.description: Tap a glass bottle with a spoon. The glass wall shakes, and the water inside shakes with it. More water means more weight to shake, so the note is lower. Now blow across the top. What shakes is the air in the bottle. A bottle with a narrow neck acts like a spring of air with a plug of air in the neck. Less air inside means a stiffer spring, so the note is higher. More water means less air, so a fuller bottle gives a higher note when you blow. In a wider pipe the rule is easier: the air column vibrates at about the speed of sound divided by four times its length, so a shorter air column gives a higher note. The same bottle and the same water give opposite orders because different things are shaking. Helmholtz used glass bottles of different sizes in the 1860s to pick out single overtones from a complex sound. They are still called Helmholtz resonators. They also explain why a conch shell sounds like the sea. The shell is a cavity, and noise from the room makes the air inside resonate, at the pitch that fits the shell. The sound is not the sea at all. A bigger shell gives a deeper sound.
examples: A big steel drum booms low and a small tin rings high, when blown across or tapped, because bigger spaces have lower natural notes.
Put your ear to a steel tumbler or a katori, and you hear a faint rushing. It is the noise of the room, with the pitch that fits the space inside.
A jug filling up from a tap rises in pitch as the air above the water gets shorter. You can tell how full it is by listening.
explanations.art: A glass bottle drawn twice: on the left being tapped with a spoon, with the glass wall and water shaking, and on the right being blown across, with the air column shaking.
explanations.context: In the earlier unit you tapped glasses with different amounts of water. This card explains why blowing across the same bottles reverses the order.

explanations.concept: Sound from moving air: whistles, flutes and singing wires
explanations.definition: When a stream of air hits a sharp edge, it swirls from side to side, and the swirls make a tone. This is called an edge tone. A flute or a whistle makes its note by joining an edge tone to an air column.
explanations.description: Blow a thin stream of air across a sharp edge, such as the rim of a bottle or the lip hole of a bansuri. The stream does not flow smoothly. It flips to one side of the edge, then the other, and makes little swirls called vortexes. Each flip pushes the air around it. The flips repeat many times a second, and that is a tone. Blowing faster makes the flips faster, so the pitch rises. In a flute or a bottle, the edge tone is joined to the air column. The air column picks out a few pitches where it resonates, and the edge tone locks onto one of them. That is why you can change a flute note by blowing harder: the edge tone jumps to a higher resonance. Wires hum in the wind in the same way. In 1878 the Czech physicist Vincenc Strouhal studied this and found that the pitch depends on the wind speed and the thickness of the wire. Thin wires in a fast wind give a higher hum. Bamboo clumps, electric wires, tall chimneys and railings can all sing in the wind. The same swirls explain why a cut bamboo or a hollow pole sometimes moans on a windy night. The wind is not making a song. It is flipping from side to side at an edge, and the space inside is picking out one note.
examples: A bansuri player blows a thin stream of air against the sharp edge of the blowing hole. Changing how hard they blow can move the note up by a whole octave.
Overhead wires can hum on a windy day. The thicker the wire, the lower the hum.
A cut bamboo pole with a hole in it can moan on a windy night, because the air inside is excited by the wind blowing over the edge.
explanations.art: A stream of air from a person's lips striking the sharp edge of a bansuri blowing hole, with small swirls on both sides, and a wire in the wind with a line of swirls trailing behind.
explanations.context: A flute has no string and no skin, so what shakes? This card explains how a stream of air hitting an edge makes a note.

explanations.concept: Pops, cracks and booms: a sound without a steady vibration
explanations.definition: A pop is one sudden push on the air, a pressure pulse. It spreads as a short bang that mixes many pitches, and not as a steady note.
explanations.description: A clap squeezes the air between your palms, and the squeezed air bursts out through the gaps. That one push is the clap. A balloon bursts and the stretched rubber snaps back in a fraction of a second. A firecracker releases a lot of gas at once. In each case the push is short and has no steady pitch. Scientists call such a sound noise, because it holds many pitches mixed together. If you cup your hands, the clap has a hollow pop with a pitch, because the cupped space is a small resonator. Thunder is a bigger pop. Lightning heats the air in its path to tens of thousands of degrees in a split second. The air expands faster than sound can move away, and this makes a shock wave. The shock wave spreads out and slows into the rumble that we hear. Light travels almost instantly, but sound moves about a kilometre in three seconds, so you can count the seconds between the flash and the thunder to find how far away the lightning was. A whip crack is also a shock wave. A loop runs along the whip and speeds up, until the tip moves faster than the speed of sound, and what you hear is a small boom. Scientists worked this out with high-speed photographs and, in 2002, a computer model. In water, the snapping shrimp closes a claw so fast that a bubble forms and then collapses with a loud bang. The bang can stun small fish. In 2001 scientists found that the collapsing bubble also gives off a tiny flash of light.
examples: Cupped hands give a lower, hollow clap than flat hands, because the cupped space picks out a pitch.
Count the seconds between a lightning flash and the thunder, and divide by three to get the distance in kilometres.
Popping a paper bag is a short push of air, and a bigger bag gives a deeper pop.
explanations.art: A pair of hands clapping with a ring of squeezed air spreading out, beside a lightning bolt with a larger ring, and a tiny shrimp in a rock pool with a bubble and a flash.
explanations.context: Not every sound is a steady note. This card looks at pops, cracks and booms, which are made by one sudden push on the air.

explanations.concept: Squeaks and screeches: sticking and slipping
explanations.definition: A squeak happens when two surfaces rub, stick, slip, and stick again, over and over, very fast. The jerks make the surfaces vibrate, and they push the air.
explanations.description: Drag your finger across a window. If the finger is dry, it drags and makes almost no sound. If it is very wet, it glides and makes no sound either. But if the finger is just a little damp, it squeaks. Here is why. The finger grips the glass, and your hand keeps pushing, so the skin stretches a little. When the push is strong enough, the finger slips forward. Then it grips again. It does this hundreds or thousands of times each second. Each jerk is a tiny vibration. A squeak needs the grip to be strong enough to stick and weak enough to slip. This middle zone of friction is why oil stops a squeaky hinge: oil makes the grip too weak to stick. A violin bow works the same way. Rosin, a sticky powder, makes the bow grip the string, pull it sideways, and then let go, again and again. The string vibrates at its own natural pitch, because it is the string's pitch that decides when it slips. A cricket makes sound by rubbing a rough edge on one wing across a row of ridges on the other wing, like running a nail along a comb. Scientists have found that crickets chirp faster when the weather is warmer. Cicadas make their loud calls with a ribbed plate on their body that clicks in and out, like pressing the lid of a tin.
examples: A door hinge squeaks until a drop of oil makes it slide smoothly.
Chalk on a board can screech, because it sticks and slips along the board.
A wet finger on the rim of a glass can make the glass sing, because the finger sticks and slips at the glass's own natural pitch.
explanations.art: A finger on a window with a magnified view of the skin gripping and slipping in tiny jumps, and a violin bow on a string with the same sticking and slipping drawn beside it.
explanations.context: A squeak seems to come from nowhere. This card explains how rubbing makes a sound, and why it only happens when the grip is just right.

explanations.concept: A voice is a buzz shaped by a space
explanations.definition: Your voice starts as a buzz from the vocal folds, which holds many overtones. The throat, mouth and nose shape the buzz by making some overtones louder than others. The shaping makes the vowels.
explanations.description: Your vocal folds are two soft flaps in your throat. Air from your lungs pushes them apart and they snap shut again, over and over. That makes a buzz of about 100 to 400 times each second, with many strong overtones. The buzz alone sounds like a raw, nasal hum. Then your throat, mouth and nose act like a bottle. They have natural pitches, and they make the overtones near those pitches louder. When you change the shape of your mouth, you change which overtones are boosted. This is how you make different vowels. 'Ee' has a narrow space at the front of the mouth, 'oo' has a round one. Try singing one note and changing the vowel slowly. The pitch stays the same, but the vowel changes. This is called the source and filter idea. It was worked out by the Swedish scientist Gunnar Fant in 1960. A whisper shows it clearly. When you whisper, the vocal folds do not buzz. Instead, air rushes through a narrow gap in your throat and makes a hiss. The hiss has no pitch, but your mouth shapes it, so a listener can still hear 'ee' and 'oo'. Singers in Tuva, in Siberia, use the same idea. They shape their mouth so tightly that one overtone is picked out of the buzz and sounds like a separate whistle above the low drone. Songbirds have a voice box deep in their chest, with two sides. Each side can make its own sound, so a bird can sing two notes at once.
examples: Sing one steady note and change from 'ee' to 'aa' to 'oo'. The pitch stays the same and the vowel changes.
Put your fingers on your throat. Hum, and you feel a buzz. Whisper, and you feel nothing, yet you can still be understood.
Pinch your nose and say 'mama'. The nose is part of the filter, so the sound changes.
explanations.art: A side view of a head with vocal folds buzzing at the throat, and the throat and mouth space shown as a bottle shape, with three different mouth shapes giving three vowels.
explanations.context: In the earlier unit you learned that your vocal folds vibrate. This card shows how the rest of your head shapes that buzz into words.

explanations.concept: Why do some pairs of notes sound sweet?
explanations.description: Some pairs of notes sound smooth and pleasing together, and some sound rough and tense. Musicians in many places have noticed this, and the simplest ratios, like 2 to 1 for the octave and 3 to 2 for Sa and Pa, tend to sound sweet. But scientists do not agree on why. The answer may be in the physics of the sound, in the way the ear works, or in what we have learned from the music around us.
examples: Sa and Pa played together on a tanpura sound very settled. Sa and a note just a little above it sound rough and buzzy.
Two strings that are slightly out of tune with each other make a slow wobble in loudness, called beats.

perspectives.who: Pythagoras and his followers in ancient Greece, as reported by later writers
perspectives.explanation: Notes sound sweet when their string lengths make simple ratios, like 2 to 1 and 3 to 2. The world is built on numbers, and the sweetness is a sign of this.
Two notes close together make beats, a fast wobble that sounds rough. Notes sound sweet when their overtones do not beat against each other. The ear is the judge.

perspectives.who: Josh McDermott and his team, in 2016
perspectives.explanation: They tested the Tsimane people of Bolivia, who live far from Western music, and found that they did not prefer sweet pairs to rough pairs as Western listeners do. This suggests that learning from the music we hear plays a big part.

perspectives.who: Indian music theory, for example in the Natyashastra of Bharata
perspectives.explanation: Certain pairs of notes, such as Sa and Pa, are called samvadi, which means they agree. The theory explains how to build a scale from such pairs and from small steps called shrutis.

explanations.art: Two tanpura strings played together with a smooth line between them, and two slightly mistuned strings with a wobbly line between them.
explanations.context: We found simple ratios for notes that blend. This card asks the question that science has not settled: why do those notes feel sweet?

agreed.text: Pitch is the number of vibrations each second, counted in hertz. A higher pitch is a faster vibration.
agreed.evidence: Vibrations can be counted with a stroboscope, with a microphone and a screen, and in slow strings by eye. Whatever the source, the pitch we hear matches the count.

chart.title: How many times each second some things vibrate (about)
chart.note: Numbers are rounded. Real voices and wings vary from one to another.

agreed.text: Halving the length of a string or an air column makes the note one octave higher. A string or pipe vibrates faster when shorter, tighter or thinner.
agreed.evidence: Marin Mersenne wrote down these rules in 1636. Instrument makers in every part of the world use them, and they match the frequencies measured by modern instruments.

agreed.text: A plucked string, a played pipe and a plate vibrate in many ways at once. The mix of these overtones gives the sound its timbre.
agreed.evidence: Hermann von Helmholtz picked out overtones with bottle resonators in 1863. Modern spectrum analysers show them as separate peaks for every instrument.

agreed.text: Air moving past an edge can make a tone, and the space it blows into picks the note. A pop is one sudden push of air with no steady pitch.
agreed.evidence: A bottle, a flute and a whistle all work this way. A pop recorded on a screen shows one sharp spike and a jumble of pitches, not a regular wave.

agreed.text: A squeak comes from stick-slip. Two surfaces grip, slip and grip again many times each second, and the squeak stops if the grip is too strong or too weak.
agreed.evidence: A finger on glass squeaks only when damp, and not when dry or wet. High-speed cameras show surfaces moving in tiny jumps while a squeak sounds.

agreed.text: A voice is a buzz from the vocal folds that is shaped by the throat, mouth and nose. A whisper has no buzz, yet its vowels can be heard.
agreed.evidence: Gunnar Fant published this source and filter picture in 1960. X-ray and scanner pictures show the mouth taking the shape of each vowel.

challenging.claim: High notes travel faster than low notes.
challenging.who: Greek thinkers such as Archytas of Tarentum, about 400 BCE, and others after him
challenging.for: A high note feels quick and sharp. A low note feels slow and heavy. It seems that a quick feeling should travel quickly.
challenging.against: In the 1630s Marin Mersenne listened to sounds across a distance and reported that high and low notes arrive at the same moment. Pitch is the number of vibrations each second, and not the speed of travel.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that high and low sounds travel at different speeds.

challenging.claim: Every sound is a steady vibration with one pitch.
challenging.who: A natural thing to think after learning that sound is vibration
challenging.for: Tuning forks, strings and flutes all make a steady note that we can hum along with.
challenging.against: A clap, a pop, a hiss and a crash are not steady. They are one sudden push or a jumble of many pitches. Even a flute note holds many overtones at once.
challenging.context: This card is about whether all sounds are steady notes.

challenging.claim: A whisper is just a softer version of your normal voice.
challenging.for: A whisper is quiet and uses the same mouth and words as speech.
challenging.against: When you whisper, your vocal folds do not buzz. Air rushes through a gap in the throat and hisses. You can feel the difference by touching your throat. The mouth still shapes the hiss into vowels.
challenging.context: This card is about what a whisper really is.

challenging.claim: A flute's wall material, such as silver or wood, changes the tone of the note.
challenging.for: Players say they can feel and hear a difference between a silver flute and a gold one or a wooden one.
challenging.against: In 1971 the physicist John Coltman made flutes with walls of different materials and found that listeners could not reliably tell them apart. The shape of the air column matters most. Some players and makers still disagree.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the stuff a flute is made of changes its sound.

challenging.claim: Notes sound sweet together because simple ratios are pleasing to everyone, everywhere.
challenging.who: Followers of Pythagoras and many later writers
challenging.for: Octaves and fifths sound settled in music from many places, and they match simple ratios.
challenging.against: In 2016 a team led by Josh McDermott found that the Tsimane people of Bolivia, who live far from Western music, did not prefer sweet pairs of notes to rough ones. What counts as sweet may be partly learned.
challenging.context: This card is about why some pairs of notes sound sweet, and whether it is the same for everybody.

big_questions.q: A bottle gives opposite orders of notes when it is tapped and when it is blown across. So where does the note belong, to the bottle, to the water or to the way it is played?
big_questions.hint: Think about what shakes in each case. Is the water the same thing in both?

big_questions.q: A whisper has no buzz from the throat, yet we hear vowels in it. What exactly is a voice?
big_questions.hint: Think about the two parts: what makes the buzz, and what shapes it.

big_questions.q: A finger squeaks on a window only when it is damp, and not when it is dry or wet. What does this say about how the world sticks together and slips apart?
big_questions.hint: Think of a hinge, a violin bow and a cricket. All of them depend on the middle of the grip.

big_questions.q: A pop contains every pitch at once, and a pure note contains only one. Which is more natural?
big_questions.hint: Think of the sounds in a forest, a market and a school. How many are pure notes?

big_questions.q: A bottle sings because of the empty space inside it. Is the empty part of a thing part of the thing?
big_questions.hint: Think of a bansuri without its hollow, or a jar with no inside.

big_questions.q: A snapping shrimp makes a bubble that collapses with a flash of light. Where does the light come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the energy of a sudden squeeze.

big_questions.q: A whole village once thought a moaning verandah was a ghost. How could you prove that a sound has an ordinary cause, and what would convince you?
big_questions.hint: Think about stopping the sound, changing it on purpose and making it again.

big_questions.q: People in different parts of the world find different music sweet. Is there a music that every human would love?
big_questions.hint: Think of what the Tsimane people of Bolivia showed, and what you hear at weddings, temples and cinemas.

story.title: The Moan in the Courtyard
story.note: Valli, Aachi, Muthu Thatha, Meena, Karthik and the house are made up. Chettinad is a real region of Tamil Nadu with huge old houses and open courtyards. The science is real. Wind across the mouth of a large jar can make a moaning note. The note is set by the length of the air column, and pouring in water shortens the air column and raises the note.
text: Valli came to her grandmother's house in Karaikudi for the summer holidays. It was a huge old house in Chettinad, with forty rooms, tall wooden pillars and a courtyard open to the sky in the middle. Her grandmother, Aachi, had lived there all her life.
At the back of the house there was a long verandah. Along its wall stood six big clay jars, taller than Valli, where the family kept rainwater.

On her second evening, when the hot wind began to blow from the south, Valli heard it. A long, low moan, like a very sad person singing one note. Ooooooo. It rose a little, then faded. Then it came back.

'Don't go to the back verandah after dark,' said Muthu Thatha, the old watchman, with a shiver. 'My father said it is a spirit.' Her cousins Karthik and Meena, who were eight and seven, pulled their blankets up to their noses.
Valli did not pull up a blanket. She sat with her chin on her knees and listened. 'A ghost has nothing that shakes,' she thought. 'But every sound has something that shakes. So what is shaking?'
The next evening she took a torch, a pencil and her notebook, and she asked Muthu Thatha to come with her. He grumbled all the way. 'I only come because you are my Aachi's granddaughter,' he said.

On the verandah the moan was louder. Valli walked slowly along the wall with one hand cupped behind her ear. At the third jar it was strongest. She shone her torch into the dark mouth of the jar. She saw only a little rainwater, far below.

'Thatha, please hold the torch.' Valli put her palm flat over the mouth of the jar. The moan stopped at once. She took her palm away, and the moan began again. 'The ghost lives in the jar,' whispered Muthu Thatha. 'No,' said Valli. 'The wind lives in the jar.'

She remembered the feeling of blowing across the top of a bottle. She leaned over, pursed her lips, and blew across the mouth of the jar. Hooo. A deep note came back, a little like the moan. Muthu Thatha's eyebrows rose to the top of his head.
'But why only this jar?' he asked. 'And why only in the south wind?' It was a good question, and Valli did not know the answer yet. She wrote it in her notebook and went to bed.

In the morning she counted the water in the jars. The third jar was nearly empty. The others were full almost to the top. 'In school we blew across bottles with water in them,' she said at breakfast. 'The more water, the higher the note. A long column of air makes a low note, and a short one makes a high note.'

'So the third jar has the longest column of air,' she went on. 'It sings the lowest, and the wind finds it. The full jars have short columns of air. Their notes are too high and thin for this wind.' Aachi, who was peeling a mango, stopped. 'Then if we pour in a bucket of water...' 'The ghost will sing higher,' said Valli.

They tried it that afternoon. Muthu Thatha carried the bucket himself. One bucket went in, and Valli blew across the jar. Hooo, a little higher. A second bucket. Higher still. When the jar was half full, Muthu Thatha blew across it himself, puffing out his cheeks like a conch player, and a clear, bright note came out. He laughed so hard that he had to sit down on the step.

That evening the south wind came, as usual. The third jar did not moan. It sang a lighter note, almost cheerful. Meena and Karthik stood at the end of the verandah, listening, and their blankets lay forgotten on the floor.

Valli had an idea. With Muthu Thatha's help she poured different amounts of water into three of the jars, and left the others. On the next windy evening the verandah did not moan. It played. Three notes rose and fell as the wind came and went, sometimes alone, sometimes together, like an old orchestra tuning up.

'In seventy years in this house, I never knew it was waiting to be tuned,' said Aachi. Muthu Thatha, who had once been afraid of the verandah, now sat on the step every evening with a glass of tea, and called it Valli's raagam. And on the last night of the holidays, Valli slid a lid over the mouth of the last jar and lifted it, once, twice, three times, to hear the house go silent and sing again.
story.epiphany: For the parent: wind blowing across the mouth of the jar sets the air inside shaking, as it does when you blow across a bottle. The note is set by the length of the air column, so the jar with the most air gave the lowest moan. Pouring in water shortens the air column and raises the note. Covering the mouth stops the moan. The sound was not in the wind or in the clay. It came from the empty space shaped by the jar. Valli proved it by stopping the sound, changing it on purpose and making it again.
ask: Why did the moan stop when Valli put her palm over the mouth of the jar?
Why did the note get higher when water was poured into the jar?
Why did the jar with the most air in it give the lowest note?
What did Valli do to show that the sound had an ordinary cause?
Where in your home might wind or breath across an opening make a sound?

roots.context: We have found four ways to start a sound, and seen that the space around a source shapes the sound as much as the source does. Now we ask what that says about where a sound belongs, and about what is empty.

deep_truth.truth: In the whisper test, listeners still told 'ee' from 'oo' with no buzz from the throat. Only a hiss left the throat, and the mouth shaped it. In the bottle test, tapping and blowing gave opposite orders of notes. So a sound belongs to what starts it and to the space that shapes it.
deep_truth.habit: We say a sound comes from its source: the drum, the string or the throat. But the same source sounds different when the space around it changes. So the source alone does not fix the sound.
deep_truth.evidence: The same bottle and the same water gave opposite orders of notes, depending on whether it was tapped or blown across. In a whisper, the vowels came from the mouth's shape alone.

three.who_am_i: Your voice is a buzz in your throat shaped by the space in your head. Your voice belongs to your whole body, and no part of it makes it alone.
three.what_is_life: A songbird has a voice box with two sides and sings two notes at once. A cricket rubs his wings. A snapping shrimp pops a bubble. Living beings make sounds in many ways, and use the shapes of their bodies to do it.
three.what_is_this_world: A jar, a throat and a flute sing with the same air. The note comes from how the air is pushed and how the empty space is shaped.

roots.thread: A string, a skin, a stream of air and a squeeze all push on the air. The air is the same air in every case. What changes is how it is pushed and what empty space it is in. A bottle, a throat, a hall and a flute are all emptiness with a shape, and the shape picks out the notes. So the empty part of a thing is as much a part of its sound as the solid part. Where one stops and the other begins is hard to say.

teachings.teaching: Clay is shaped into a pot, and it is the empty space inside that makes the pot useful. We profit from what is there, and we use what is not there.
teachings.link: A clay jar moans only because of the air inside it. The jar gives the shape, and the emptiness gives the note.

teachings.teaching: When a drum is beaten, we cannot grasp the sounds as they spread out. But if we grasp the drum or the person who beats it, we have grasped the sound. The text gives the same teaching for a conch and a vina.
teachings.link: This unit finds that a sound cannot be understood apart from what makes it and the space that shapes it. The Upanishad points to the same unity.

teachings.teaching: This is the opening of an old Indian study of the sounds of speech. It names the parts of a spoken sound: the letter, the pitch, the length, the strength, the evenness and the joining.
teachings.link: Indian teachers studied for centuries how the mouth shapes speech. Today's source and filter picture of the voice finds the same two parts.

science.text: The voice has a source, the buzz of the vocal folds, and a filter, the shape of the throat, mouth and nose. A whisper uses a hiss as its source.
Why some pairs of notes sound sweet to nearly everyone is not settled. Physics, the ear and learning may all play a part.

other_view.view: A sound is a pattern of pressure in the air, wherever it is. What started it and what shaped it are its history, and the pattern itself is all there is. Asking where a sound belongs does not add anything to what a microphone measures.

practice.title: Hum and shape
practice.say: Sit comfortably and breathe in slowly. Hum one steady note with your lips closed, and feel the buzz in your lips and face. Now slowly open your mouth, and let the hum slide from 'mm' to 'ooo' and then to 'eee', without changing the note. Notice how the same buzz becomes different sounds. Close your mouth again and hum for three more breaths.
practice.kid: Hum one note. Slowly open your mouth. Change from 'mm' to 'oo' to 'ee'. The note stays. The sound changes.

ask: When you speak, where does your voice live: in the throat, in the mouth, or in both?
Is the empty part inside a bottle part of the bottle?
If the same buzz can become many different vowels, what else do we call different that might be the same thing shaped differently?
roots.art: A child humming with her mouth shaping 'oo', with a faint glowing buzz in her throat and shapes of three different mouths floating above.

how_we_found_out.story: More than 2,300 years ago, Greek thinkers such as Archytas of Tarentum taught that high notes travel faster than low notes. It seemed right. A high note feels quick and sharp, and a low note feels slow and heavy. In the 1630s two men tested it. In France, a priest and scientist called Marin Mersenne listened to sounds from far away. High notes and low notes reached him at the same moment, so they travel at the same speed. He also stretched a very long string until it was slow enough to count its swings. He found rules for how length changes the count, and used the rules to work out how fast short strings swing. In Italy, Galileo scraped a sharp chisel over a brass plate and found fine lines scratched into it. Close lines made a high squeal and wide lines made a low one. A high note is not a fast traveller. It is a fast vibration.
how_we_found_out.who: Marin Mersenne, a French priest and scientist (1588 to 1648), and Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist (1564 to 1642)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Greek thinkers, including Archytas, taught that high notes travel faster than low notes. Mersenne and Galileo showed that all notes travel at the same speed, and that pitch is the number of vibrations each second.

games.title: Source Sorter: shake, blow, pop or rub?
games.context: This is a sorting game. Each card names a sound you know. You decide how that sound is started, and then say why.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile on a table, and eight tokens in two sets of four, each token showing one of four ways to make a sound.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A reader holding up a card that says 'A damp finger squeaks on a window' and three players each putting a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else puts a token face down.

setup.art: Tokens turned face up together, and the reader turning the card over to show the answer.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. The reader reads the answer on the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a sound you know on the front, and how it is started on the back

items.f: A sitar string is plucked and rings.
items.b: SOLID SHAKES. The string shakes and pushes the air around it.

items.f: A temple bell is struck.
items.b: SOLID SHAKES. The whole bell shakes for a long time.

items.f: A tabla skin is tapped with the fingers.
items.b: SOLID SHAKES. The stretched skin vibrates and pushes the air.

items.f: A person hums with their lips closed.
items.b: SOLID SHAKES. The vocal folds buzz, and the head shapes the buzz.

items.f: A tuning fork is tapped on a knee.
items.b: SOLID SHAKES. The two prongs shake back and forth.

items.f: A phone buzzes on a table.
items.b: SOLID SHAKES. A small motor shakes the phone, and the phone shakes the table.

items.f: A bansuri is played.
items.b: AIR SHAKES IN A SPACE. A stream of air hits an edge, and the air column inside picks the note.

items.f: Someone blows across the top of a bottle.
items.b: AIR SHAKES IN A SPACE. The air in the bottle vibrates, and the amount of air sets the note.

items.f: A conch shell is blown.
items.b: AIR SHAKES IN A SPACE. The player's buzzing lips set the air inside the shell shaking.

items.f: Wind moans across the top of an old hollow pole.
items.b: AIR SHAKES IN A SPACE. Wind flips from side to side at the edge, and the air inside picks the note.

items.f: A police constable blows a whistle.
items.b: AIR SHAKES IN A SPACE. The air stream hits an edge in the whistle and sets the air inside shaking.

items.f: A child whistles with rounded lips.
items.b: AIR SHAKES IN A SPACE. The air flips at the lip's edge, and the mouth is the air space.

items.f: A balloon bursts.
items.b: SUDDEN POP. The stretched rubber snaps and the air gets one sudden push.

items.f: Two hands clap.
items.b: SUDDEN POP. The air between the palms is squeezed out in one push.

items.f: Thunder rumbles after a lightning flash.
items.b: SUDDEN POP. Lightning heats the air so fast that it makes a shock wave.

items.f: A whip is cracked.
items.b: SUDDEN POP. The tip moves faster than sound for a moment and makes a small shock wave.

items.f: A firecracker goes off down the road.
items.b: SUDDEN POP. A lot of gas is released at once. It is also loud enough to hurt your ears, so stay far away.

items.f: A paper bag full of air is hit with a hand.
items.b: SUDDEN POP. The bag bursts and the air rushes out in one push.

items.f: A door hinge squeaks as the door opens.
items.b: RUB: STICK AND SLIP. The metal parts grip, slip and grip again very fast.

items.f: A damp finger squeaks on a window.
items.b: RUB: STICK AND SLIP. The skin grips and slips on the glass hundreds of times each second.

items.f: A cricket sings in the evening.
items.b: RUB: STICK AND SLIP. A rough edge on one wing is rubbed across ridges on the other.

items.f: A bow is drawn across a violin string.
items.b: RUB: STICK AND SLIP. The sticky bow grips the string and lets go, and the string vibrates.

items.f: Chalk screeches on a board.
items.b: RUB: STICK AND SLIP. The chalk sticks and slips along the board.

items.f: Rubber slippers squeak on a wet bathroom floor.
items.b: RUB: STICK AND SLIP. The rubber grips and slips over the damp tiles.

printables.title: 8 tokens: two sets of four, one token for each way of making a sound

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Each player needs four tokens, one for each way. The sheet has two sets. With no printer, copy the 24 fronts and backs onto small slips by hand, or let the reader read from the page and keep the backs covered. With 3 or 4 players, write the four ways on small slips of paper.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. They pick the way they think the sound is started.
Everyone turns their token over together. Then the reader reads the back aloud.
A player who picked the right way scores 1 point. A player who also says the reason in one sentence, in their own words, scores 1 more.
The next player becomes the reader. Keep going until the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: you are the reader and the player. Read the front, put your token on the table, say your reason out loud, then read the back. Try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Read the four ways on the tokens aloud once.
flow.say: There are four ways to start a sound. A solid thing shakes. Air shakes in a space. There is a sudden pop. Or two things rub, stick and slip. Each card fits one way.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Read the four ways.
flow.context: This is the first step of Source Sorter. You set up the game and meet the four ways to make a sound.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who got a point, and who can give a reason?
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What is the same about every sound where a solid thing shakes?
good: Something solid moves back and forth.
You could feel it vibrate if you touched it.
It pushes the air next to it.

flow.parent: Some players find 'air shakes in a space' hard to tell from 'solid shakes' for instruments like the bansuri. Ask them where the shaking is. In a bansuri, it is the air inside the tube.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next six cards. When a player picks the wrong token, ask them to say which clue in the card made them choose it.
flow.say: A wrong token is useful. Which clue made you choose it? Let us find the clue that points to the other way.
flow.kid: Play six more cards. If you were wrong, find the clue you missed.

ask.q: How can you tell a sudden pop from a rub?
good: A pop is one push, and a rub is many tiny pushes.
A rub keeps going while you rub.
A pop is over very quickly.

flow.context: In this step, you play more cards and learn to use clues to choose.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards. Keep score on the score sheet. Skip the reasons if time is short and score only the right way.
flow.say: Now the last twelve. Keep your score. Remember to say why in one sentence.
flow.kid: Play the last twelve cards. Write down your score.

check.q: A story says that a hollow bamboo pole moans in the wind. Which way fits best?
options: Air shakes in a space
Sudden pop
Solid shakes
check.why: The wind flips from side to side at the edge of the opening, and the air inside the pole picks the note. Choosing 'solid shakes' forgets that the bamboo itself is hardly moving.

flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards and keep your score.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Ask each player which way was hardest to tell apart. Ask for a sound that uses two ways at once, such as a violin.
flow.say: Add up your scores. Which way was hardest to spot? Can you think of a sound that uses two ways together?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Think of a sound that uses two ways.

ask.q: Which instrument or sound uses more than one way to make its sound?
good: A violin: the bow rubs and sticks, and the string shakes.
A conch: lips buzz and the air inside shakes.
A voice: the vocal folds shake and the mouth shapes the air.

flow.context: This is the last step of Source Sorter. You count points and find sounds that use more than one way.

experiments.title: Tap or Blow: which way do the notes go?
experiments.question: Bottles with different amounts of water give notes in one order when you tap them. Do they give the same order when you blow across them?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will tapping and blowing put the bottles in the same order from the lowest note to the highest? Which bottle will give the highest note when tapped, and which when blown? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use five bottles of the same kind. The water amounts are the same for both tests. Tap each bottle in the same place with the same spoon. Blow across each bottle from the same distance. The listener closes their eyes and says which of two bottles gives the higher note. Each pair is tried three times. Only the way of making the sound changes, so any difference comes from tapping or blowing.
results_table: Tapping: place from lowest (1) to highest (5)
Blowing: place from lowest (1) to highest (5)

materials.item: 5 identical glass bottles with narrow necks, each holding about 250 to 300 millilitres, such as small soft-drink or juice bottles, with no chips or cracks (plastic bottles work for blowing, but not for tapping)
a measuring cup with millilitre marks
water from the tap
a wooden spoon for tapping
a folded towel to stand the bottles on
tape (any tape or a paper strip) and a pencil, to label each bottle with its water amount
a ruler, a pencil and a paper for the results table
a helper who listens with their eyes closed (with one child, the parent is the helper)

experiments.safety: Use glass bottles with no chips or cracks, and stand them on a folded towel. Tap gently with a wooden spoon, never a steel one. Wipe up spills at once. When blowing, rest between tries, and stop if anyone feels dizzy. Each child blows into their own bottle, or wipes the bottle's mouth with a clean cloth before the next child blows.

schedule.what: Guess. Fill the bottles and measure the air columns. Tap and rank. Blow and rank. Compare, and write your claim.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each way of making the sound, write the place of each bottle from lowest note to highest. Draw a line to join the water amounts to the places, once for tapping and once for blowing.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you tap and then blow across five bottles with different amounts of water, and find out whether the order of the notes stays the same.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the place of each bottle from lowest note (1) to highest (5) when blown
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers may be different. In the example, the fullest bottle gives the highest note when blown.

setup.art: Five identical glass bottles on a folded towel, with 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200 millilitres of water, being filled from a measuring cup.
setup.caption: 1. Fill five bottles with 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200 millilitres of water.

setup.art: A ruler held against a bottle, measuring from the top of the water to the mouth of the bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the air column in each bottle, from the water to the top.

setup.art: A wooden spoon tapping the side of a glass bottle halfway up, with a helper listening with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 3. Tap each bottle with the wooden spoon in the same place. The helper listens.

setup.art: A child with her lower lip against the mouth of a bottle, blowing a thin stream of air across the top.
setup.caption: 4. Blow across the top of each bottle, like blowing across a flute.

setup.art: Two lines drawn on one graph, one going up from left to right and one going down, with bottle pictures along the bottom.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a line for tapping and a line for blowing, and compare.

flow.do: Show your child the bottles and the spoon. Explain that you will tap them and then blow across them. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We have five bottles with different amounts of water. First we tap them, then we blow across them. Will the order of the notes be the same both times? Which bottle will be highest when tapped, and which when blown? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tap the bottles. Then blow across them. Is the order of notes the same? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think the order will be the same, or different?
good: It will be the same, because it is the same bottle and water.
More water makes it heavier, so lower.
I think blowing will be different, because it is air.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say the order will be the same. Write the guess at the top of the table, because the result may surprise them. Roles: with one child, you are the helper who listens and writes. With 2 to 4 children, one taps, one listens with eyes shut, one writes the table, and one blows. Swap after each bottle pair, so everyone gets a turn at tapping, blowing and listening.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tap or Blow test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Stand the bottles on the towel. Fill them with 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200 millilitres of water. Put a small piece of tape on each bottle with the amount. Measure the air column in each with the ruler and write it in the table.
flow.say: Pour the water into each bottle. Write the amount on a piece of tape. Now measure from the top of the water to the top of the bottle. That is the air column. Write each one in the table.
flow.kid: Fill the bottles. Label each one. Measure the air from the water to the top.
flow.parent: The air column gets shorter as the water goes up. If your bottles differ in size, use the same kind for all five. These amounts suit bottles of 250 to 300 millilitres. For a bigger bottle, make equal steps up to about three quarters full. Keep the water below the shoulder of the bottle. If you have fewer than five bottles, use three (for example 0, 100 and 200 millilitres) and say so.
flow.context: In this step, you fill the bottles and measure the air column in each.

flow.do: Tap each bottle halfway up with the wooden spoon, once, gently. The helper keeps their eyes shut. Play two bottles one after the other and ask which is higher. Repeat each pair three times. Then give each bottle its place.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will tap two bottles. Which note is higher, the first or the second? We will do this for every pair of neighbours, three times each. Then we can put the five in order.
flow.kid: Tap two bottles. Which is higher? Do every pair. Then put all five in order.
flow.parent: Expected: the empty bottle gives the highest tapped note, and the fullest gives the lowest. If your bottles are plastic, the difference is hard to hear, so use glass. Steps of 50 millilitres are easy to hear on glass, but if two neighbours sound alike, compare the empty bottle and the fullest one first. Real tapped notes are short and dull, so listen closely and let the helper hear each pair more than once. Write the places from 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest).

check.q: Why does the listener keep their eyes closed while the bottles are tapped?
options: So that how the bottles look does not change what they say
So the bottles ring longer
So the spoon does not slip
check.why: If the listener can see which bottle has more water, they may say what they expect. With eyes closed they must decide only from the sound. A child who picks 'ring longer' mixes up the senses.

flow.context: In this step, you tap the bottles and put them in order from lowest to highest.

flow.do: Now blow across each bottle. Rest your lower lip on the front of the bottle's mouth and blow a thin stream of air across the top. Find the position that gives a clear note. Give each bottle a place from lowest to highest in the same way.
flow.say: Touch your lower lip to the front of the bottle's mouth. Blow a thin stream of air across the top, as if you are blowing across a flute. It takes some tries. Then do the same for each bottle, and put them in order.
flow.kid: Blow across the top. Find the note. Do all five. Put them in order.
flow.parent: Blowing takes a little practice. Tilt the bottle a bit, and aim the stream of air so that it hits the far edge of the mouth. Rest between tries. If a bottle will not sing after a minute or two, try the one with the most water first, since its short air column sings more easily. A weak, airy hiss is normal at the start. Expected: the empty bottle gives the lowest blown note, and the fullest bottle gives the highest. This is the opposite of tapping.
flow.context: In this step, you blow across each bottle and put the bottles in order again.

flow.do: Compare the two orders. Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning before you explain anything.
flow.say: Look at the two orders. What do you notice? What is your claim? What is your evidence? Why do you think the orders are different? What is shaking when you tap, and what is shaking when you blow?
flow.kid: Compare the two orders. What do you notice? What is shaking each time?

ask.q: What changed between tapping and blowing, if the bottles and water stayed the same?
good: What is shaking changed.
When you tap, the glass shakes. When you blow, the air shakes.
The air column is the part that matters when blowing.

ask.q: Why does more water give a higher note when you blow?
good: There is less air, so the air column is shorter.
A short air column makes a higher note.
The water takes up room that was air.

flow.parent: Do not explain the cards yet. Let your child say what they think shakes in each case. If the orders are not reversed in your test, write down what you found and try to blow again, with a thinner stream of air. Real results are not always neat.

check.q: A bottle has 200 millilitres of water in it, and another has 50 millilitres. Which gives the higher note when blown across?
options: The one with 200 millilitres
The one with 50 millilitres
They give the same note
check.why: More water means a shorter air column, and a shorter air column gives a higher note when you blow. Picking 50 millilitres is the answer for tapping, where the glass and water shake and more water is more to shake.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the two orders and say what is shaking in each case.

flow.do: Take the empty bottle. Hum slowly from a low note up to a high note, with your mouth near its opening. Listen for the note where the bottle suddenly booms.
flow.say: Hold the empty bottle by your mouth and hum slowly, from low to high. Listen for the one note where the bottle seems to answer. That is the bottle's own note.
flow.kid: Hum slowly up from low to high near the bottle. Find the note that booms.
flow.parent: The booming note is the natural note of the air in the bottle. A voice is not strong enough to make an empty bottle ring, but you should hear one note get louder. Try with the other bottles. The fuller ones boom at higher notes. If the empty bottle's note is too low for your voice, try the fuller bottles first. The boom is gentle, so hold the bottle's mouth close to your lips and keep the room quiet. If you hear nothing, that is a fair result too, so write it down and move on.
flow.context: In this step, you use your own voice to find the bottle's natural note.

experiments.title: The Squeak Test: when does a finger squeak on glass?
experiments.question: A finger moved across a window can squeak. Does it squeak when it is dry, damp, very wet, soapy or oily?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which finger will squeak the loudest? Which will not squeak at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same clean glass, the same finger, the same gentle press and the same speed every time. Move the finger across about 20 centimetres of glass in about one second. Clean the glass between conditions. Each condition is tried three times, and a listener with eyes shut scores the squeak from 0 to 5. Only the wetness of the finger changes, so any difference comes from that.

materials.item: a clean window pane that you can reach safely at ground level, or a large mirror, or a glass table top, or a clean glass plate
a small bowl of plain water
a small bowl of water with a few drops of dish soap or hand wash
a saucer with a drop of cooking oil (a little coconut or any kitchen oil)
a soft cloth or tissue to dry and clean the glass
a paper and a pencil for the results table
a helper who listens with their eyes closed (with one child, the parent is the helper)

experiments.safety: Use a window at ground level, never near a ledge or an open balcony edge. Press gently, because glass can crack or cut. Do not use a cracked or chipped pane. Wipe up any water, soap or oil from the glass and the floor at once, because they make the floor slippery. If anyone has sensitive skin or an allergy to soap or oil, skip that condition and wash hands after.

schedule.what: Guess. Clean the glass. Test the five finger conditions three times each. Score and compare. Write your claim.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with a score from 0 (silent) to 5 (loud squeak) for each try. Then add the three scores for each condition and rank the conditions.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out which finger condition makes a squeak on glass, and which makes none.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: total squeak score for each finger condition (out of 15)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers may be different. In the example, a damp finger squeaks the most.

setup.art: A child's finger resting on a clean window pane, with a helper holding a cloth beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Clean the glass. Rest one finger gently on it.

setup.art: A finger being dipped in a bowl of water, then shaken until it is only slightly damp.
setup.caption: 2. Make the finger damp. Dip it, and shake off the drops.

setup.art: A finger moving across the glass in a straight line of about twenty centimetres, with a clock showing one second.
setup.caption: 3. Move the finger across about 20 centimetres in one second.

setup.art: A helper with eyes closed holding up fingers to show a score from zero to five.
setup.caption: 4. The helper listens with eyes closed and gives a score from 0 to 5.

flow.do: Show your child the glass and the five finger conditions: dry, damp, very wet, soapy and oily. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will drag a finger across clean glass five ways. Dry. Damp. Very wet. Soapy. Oily. Which will squeak loudest? Which will not squeak at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five kinds of finger on glass. Which squeaks loudest? Which is silent? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that finger will squeak the most?
good: A wet finger sticks to glass.
A dry finger grips the most.
Soap makes a noise like bubbles.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say a dry finger will squeak most, because it grips most. Write the guess at the top of the table. Roles: with one child, you are the listener and scorer. With 2 to 4 children, one drags the finger, one listens with eyes shut, and one writes the scores. Swap roles after each condition. If each child uses their own finger on the same condition, compare the scores. Fingers differ, which is why one finger is used for a fair test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squeak Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Clean the glass with the cloth and let it dry. Practise one smooth sweep of about 20 centimetres in one second, with a dry finger. The helper shuts their eyes and gives a score from 0 to 5. Write it as the first dry try.
flow.say: Clean the glass first. Now place one finger and drag it across the glass in about one second, with a gentle press. The listener closes their eyes and gives a score for the squeak, from nothing to very loud.
flow.kid: Clean the glass. Drag a dry finger across in one second. Give a score.
flow.parent: A dry finger makes a faint scrape or no squeak. Press the same way each time. A harder press changes the sound, so keep it gentle. Before you begin, wash and dry the finger once. Clean fingers and clean glass matter most. If glass or fingers are greasy, nothing will squeak. In very damp weather the glass may mist, so wipe it dry with the cloth before each try.
flow.context: In this step, you clean the glass and test a dry finger.

flow.do: Test the damp finger three times, then the very wet finger three times. Dip the finger and shake off the drops for damp. Let it drip for very wet. Wipe the glass between tries. Write the scores.
flow.say: For a damp finger, dip it and shake off the drops. For a very wet finger, leave the drops on. Do three sweeps each and give scores. Wipe the glass between tries.
flow.kid: Test a damp finger and a very wet finger. Wipe the glass each time. Give scores.
flow.parent: Expected: a damp finger squeaks loudly. A very wet finger glides with almost no sound. The squeak only happens when the finger sticks and slips. If even the damp finger is silent, the glass or finger is probably greasy. Wash the finger with soap, clean the glass with a damp cloth and dry it, then try again. A clean steel plate or a mirror also works. A few tries may be needed to find how damp is right. If your results differ, write what you hear.

check.q: Why must the glass be wiped between each try?
options: So that wetness left from the last try does not change the next one
So the glass shines
So the helper can see better
check.why: A damp finger leaves a film of water on the glass. If it stays, the next condition is no longer the one you think it is. Wiping makes each try start in the same way.

flow.context: In this step, you test the damp and very wet finger.

flow.do: Test the soapy finger three times and the oily finger three times. Wipe the glass between tries and wash the finger after. Write the scores. Add up the three scores for each condition.
flow.say: Dip the finger in the soapy water for the soapy test. Use a touch of oil on the finger for the oily test. Do three sweeps for each and give scores. Wipe the glass well after the oil.
flow.kid: Test a soapy finger and an oily finger. Wipe the glass. Add up the scores.
flow.parent: Expected: a soapy finger may squeak, though usually less than damp, and it can also be silent. Soap films vary, so report what you hear. An oily finger is silent. Wipe the oil off the glass with a dry cloth, then a damp one, so that nobody slips.
flow.context: In this step, you test the soapy and oily finger and add up the scores.

flow.do: Compare the totals. Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning before you explain anything.
flow.say: Which finger squeaked most? Which did not squeak? What is your claim? What is your evidence? Why do you think the damp finger is different from the dry one and the very wet one?
flow.kid: Which finger squeaked most? Which was silent? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why does a damp finger squeak, but a dry or a very wet finger does not?
good: The damp finger grips and slips again and again.
A dry finger grips too much and a wet finger slips too much.
The grip has to be in the middle.

flow.parent: Do not explain the cards yet. A good answer says that squeaking needs both gripping and slipping. If the child can say 'the grip is not too much and not too little', that is the idea. To go further, use the damp finger and try three speeds (slow, medium, fast). Does the pitch of the squeak change?

check.q: A squeaky door hinge goes quiet after a drop of oil. What is the best reason?
options: The oil lets the metal slide without sticking, so the stick and slip stops
The oil makes the metal heavier
The oil makes the hinge colder
check.why: The squeak needs the metal to stick and slip over and over. Oil makes the surfaces slide smoothly, so they do not stick. A child who picks 'heavier' is thinking of weight, but a squeak is about grip.

flow.context: In this step, you compare your totals and say why the damp finger is different.

activities.title: The Four-Way Sound Hunt: shake, blow, pop or rub?

materials.item: a notebook or sheet of paper with four columns: shake, blow, pop and rub
a pencil
a steel tumbler or plate and a spoon, to tap
an empty bottle, to blow across
a door with a hinge, and a clean window or glass
a paper bag, if you have one (a plain paper bag from the kirana is fine)

activities.safety: Do not pop anything close to anyone's ear. Use a paper bag only in a room, away from other people's ears. Never use a firecracker.

schedule.what: Guess. Walk round the house and make or find at least twelve sounds. Sort them into the four columns. Find one that does not fit.

activities.record: A table with four columns and at least twelve sounds sorted into them. A note on the sound that was hardest to place.
activities.context: In this activity, you hunt for sounds around your home and sort them by how they are started: a solid shaking, air shaking in a space, a sudden pop or a rub.

setup.art: A child with a notebook and a pencil walking through a kitchen, tapping a steel tumbler and listening.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round the house with a notebook. Make or find a sound.

setup.art: A table with four columns headed shake, blow, pop and rub, with small drawings of sounds under each.
setup.caption: 2. Draw four columns and sort each sound into one of them.

setup.art: A child with a puzzled face pointing at a sound written between two columns.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the sound that is hard to place, and say why.

flow.do: Show your child the four columns. Say that sounds start in four ways. Ask which they think will hold the most sounds in the house, and why.
flow.say: We will hunt for sounds and sort them in four columns. Shake, blow, pop and rub. Which column do you think will have the most sounds in our home? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hunt for sounds. Sort them into four columns. Which will have the most? Why?

ask.q: Which column do you think will have the fewest sounds?
good: Pop, because pops are rare.
Blow, because you need a bottle.
Rub, because I do not know any.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The shake column is usually biggest and the rub column smallest. Roles: with one child, you walk round together and you write. With 2 to 4 children, each keeps their own sheet and hunts in a different room for 5 minutes, then everyone compares sheets. Count which column grew biggest. No sound needs to be loud, so ask everyone to keep the volume low for the neighbours.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Four-Way Sound Hunt. You guess before you hunt.

flow.do: Walk round the house. Make each of these sounds, and write each one in a column. Tap a tumbler. Blow across the bottle. Clap. Open the door slowly. Squeak a damp finger on the glass.
