flow.say: Make each sound and listen. Tap the tumbler. Blow across the bottle. Clap your hands. Open the door slowly. Squeak a damp finger on the glass. Which column does each one go in?
flow.kid: Tap the tumbler. Blow across the bottle. Clap. Open the door. Squeak the glass.
flow.parent: The squeaky glass needs a damp finger on clean glass. If it will not squeak, count the door or a rubbed balloon instead. Expected: tumbler in shake, bottle in blow, clap in pop, door and glass in rub. Let your child decide first. If they put the clap in shake, ask where the shaking is.

check.q: A clap goes in the pop column. What is the best reason?
options: The air between the hands gets one sudden push
The hands vibrate for a long time
The air in the room is shaking slowly
check.why: A clap squeezes the air once and lets it go. There is no steady vibration. A child who picks 'hands vibrate' is describing a tuning fork, which keeps shaking after it is hit.

flow.context: In this step, you make five sounds and sort them.

flow.do: Find at least seven more sounds and write them in the columns. Think of the fridge, the fan, the pressure cooker, the mixie, a bird at the window and your own voice.
flow.say: Find seven more sounds in the house or outside the window. Think of the fridge, the fan, the cooker, the mixie and a bird. Write each in a column. If you are not sure, write it between two columns.
flow.kid: Find seven more sounds. Put each in a column. Write between two columns if unsure.
flow.parent: Some sounds fit two columns. A pressure cooker whistle, a mixie and a bird's call are all mixed. That is fine. Ask the child where the shaking is.
flow.context: In this step, you find more sounds and sort them.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose the sound that was hardest to place, and to explain why. Ask them for their claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Which sound was the hardest to place? Why? What is your claim about how it starts? What did you notice? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which sound was hard to place? Why? What do you think starts it?

ask.q: Can one sound use two ways at once?
good: A violin: the bow rubs and the string shakes.
My voice: the vocal folds shake and the mouth shapes it.
A conch: lips buzz and the air inside shakes.

flow.context: In this step, you talk about the sound that was hardest to place.

activities.title: Whisper Vowels: can you hear 'ee' and 'oo' with no buzz?

materials.item: a sheet of cardboard or a big book, to stand up as a screen between speaker and listener
three small slips of paper marked 'ee', 'aa' and 'oo', and a bowl to draw them from
a paper and pencil to write down the answers
2 to 4 people: one speaker, one listener, and the others to score and swap in (with one child, the parent is the speaker)

schedule.what: Guess. Feel the throat for a buzz when speaking and whispering. Test the listener with spoken vowels and whispered vowels, ten each. Count the right answers.

activities.record: A table with two rows, spoken and whispered, and the number of vowels the listener got right out of ten in each row. Note the number you would expect from guessing alone.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out whether a listener can tell the vowels 'ee', 'aa' and 'oo' apart when they are whispered, with no buzz from the throat.

setup.art: A child with two fingers on her throat, saying 'aaa' out loud and then whispering 'aaa', with a small buzz drawn in the first case only.
setup.caption: 1. Touch your throat. Speak a vowel, and then whisper it. Feel the buzz.

setup.art: A cardboard screen on a table with a speaker on one side drawing a paper slip from a bowl and a listener on the other side with a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. The speaker draws a slip. The listener cannot see their mouth.

setup.art: A score sheet with a column for spoken and a column for whispered, with ten ticks in each.
setup.caption: 3. Tick each right answer. Count ten tries for spoken and ten for whispered.

flow.do: Ask your child to put two fingers on their throat and say 'aaa' out loud, then whisper 'aaa'. Ask what they feel. Then ask for a guess and reason about the test.
flow.say: Put two fingers on your throat. Say 'aaa' out loud. Now whisper 'aaa'. What do you feel? In the test, a listener will try to tell 'ee', 'aa' and 'oo' in a whisper. Can they? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Touch your throat. Say 'aaa', then whisper it. What do you feel?

ask.q: Do you think a listener will be able to tell whispered vowels apart? Why?
good: No, because there is no voice.
Yes, because the mouth is a different shape.
Only some of them.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The child should feel a buzz when speaking and none when whispering. Many children expect that whispered vowels will be hard to tell apart.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whisper Vowels. You feel the buzz, and you guess before you test.

flow.do: Set up the screen so that the listener cannot see the speaker's mouth. Put the three slips in the bowl. Explain that the speaker will draw a slip, say the vowel in a clear voice, then put the slip back.
flow.say: Put up the screen. The speaker draws a slip and says that vowel. The listener says which one it was. The speaker puts the slip back, so that each try is a new guess.
flow.kid: Put up the screen. Draw a slip. Say the vowel. The listener guesses.
flow.parent: The slips go back each time, so a vowel can come twice in a row. That is what makes it a fair test. Switch off the fan and TV, and keep the room quiet, because a whisper is easy to lose in noise. The listener sits about 2 metres away. If the listener could see the lips, they could lip-read, and the test would not show what the sound alone says.

check.q: Why is a screen needed between the speaker and the listener?
options: So the listener cannot lip-read and must use only the sound
So the speaker can speak louder
So the room is quieter
check.why: If the listener sees the mouth shapes, they may guess the vowel from the lips. The screen makes sure they use the sound only. Without it, the test would measure lip-reading.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the screen and the slips.

flow.do: Do ten spoken tries. The speaker draws a slip, says the vowel out loud at an ordinary speaking volume, and puts the slip back. The listener says which vowel it was. Tick the right answers.
flow.say: Speak the vowel in your ordinary voice. Listener, which vowel was it? We will do ten. Tick the right ones.
flow.kid: Speak the vowel. The listener guesses. Do ten tries. Tick the right ones.
flow.parent: Expected: almost all ten are right with a normal voice. Keep the volume the same on every try.
flow.context: In this step, you do ten tries with a normal voice.

flow.do: Do ten whispered tries. The speaker draws a slip and whispers the vowel with a clear mouth shape. Keep the same distance and loudness as before. Tick the right answers.
flow.say: Now whisper the vowel. Make the mouth shape clear, but do not buzz. Listener, which vowel was it? Ten tries. Tick the right ones.
flow.kid: Now whisper the vowels. Do ten tries. Tick the right ones.
flow.parent: Expected: most are right, often 8 or more out of ten, even though there is no buzz. Guessing alone would give about 3 out of 10. If the listener does badly, make sure the speaker is whispering and not softly speaking. Touch the throat to check for a buzz. These scores are typical, not promised. If the listener gets 10 out of 10 in both rows, make it harder with a longer distance, or add 'e' and 'o' slips, so that guessing alone gives about 2 out of 10.

check.q: The listener got 9 out of 10 whispered vowels right. What does that show?
options: The mouth's shape gives each vowel its sound, even with no buzz
The listener is very lucky
The throat makes the vowels
check.why: A whisper has no buzz from the vocal folds, only a hiss. The shape of the mouth boosts different parts of the hiss for each vowel. Guessing would give about 3 out of 10, so 9 is not luck.

flow.context: In this step, you do ten tries with a whisper.

flow.do: Count the right answers for each row. Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. Then ask them to try pinching their nose and saying 'mama'.
flow.say: Count the right answers for spoken and whispered. What is your claim about where vowels come from? What is your evidence? Why do you think so? Now pinch your nose and say 'mama'. What changes?
flow.kid: Count the right answers. Where do vowels come from? Pinch your nose and say 'mama'.

ask.q: If a whisper has no buzz, where do the vowels come from?
good: From the shape of the mouth.
From the way the mouth shapes the hiss.
The mouth changes the sound, not the throat.

flow.context: In this step, you count your results and say where vowels come from.
flow.parent: With a group, each child takes a turn as speaker and as listener, and you compare their scores. Different people and rooms give different scores, and that is a real result.

activities.title: The Pot That Hums Back: finding the hidden note of a space

materials.item: a large empty steel pot, bucket or deep steel vessel with a wide mouth, about 25 centimetres across and at least 20 centimetres deep (a pressure cooker pot without its lid works)
a smaller steel vessel, such as a tumbler or a small pot
a small tiled bathroom or a small room with bare walls, if you have one
a paper and pencil to record the notes
a ruler, to measure the depth of each vessel

activities.safety: Hum gently. Do not put your head inside any vessel. Hold the vessel in front of your mouth, about 5 centimetres away.

schedule.what: Guess. Measure the depth of each vessel. Hum slowly up the scale near the mouth of a big pot and find the note where it booms. Try a smaller vessel. Then try a small bathroom.

activities.record: Write which vessel boomed at which kind of note (low, middle or high). Write the depth of each vessel in centimetres. Write whether the bathroom boomed at any note.
activities.context: In this activity, you hum slowly from low to high near the mouth of a pot and find the one note where the pot seems to answer. You then try different vessels and a bathroom.

setup.art: A child holding a large steel pot in front of her mouth and humming, with faint sound lines rising from the pot at one note.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the pot near your mouth and hum slowly from low to high.

setup.art: A row of three vessels from big to small: a bucket, a pot and a tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Try each vessel. Which one booms at the lowest note?

setup.art: A child in a small tiled bathroom humming with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 3. Try a small bathroom, with the door shut.

flow.do: Show your child the big pot and the small vessel. Ask which will boom at a lower note when a person hums near it, and why.
flow.say: We will hum near the mouth of a pot, slowly from low to high. At one note the pot will answer back. Which will answer at a lower note, the big pot or the small tumbler? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hum near a pot. Find the note where it booms. Big or small, which is lower?

ask.q: Why might a big pot answer at a lower note?
good: It has more air inside.
It is like a long string.
A bigger space makes a deeper sound.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say bigger means lower. The test can show it.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Pot That Hums Back. You guess before you hum.

flow.do: Hold the big pot about 5 centimetres from your child's mouth. They hum a steady note and slowly slide it from low to high. Ask them to stop where the pot seems loudest. Write if that note was low, middle or high.
flow.say: Hold the pot near your mouth. Hum a low note and slowly slide up. Listen for the note where the pot suddenly sounds louder. That is the pot's hidden note. Stop there.
flow.kid: Hum low and slide up slowly. Listen for the note where the pot booms.
flow.parent: The booming note is the natural note of the air in the pot. Slide slowly. It may be a narrow zone of just one note. If the child's voice is not low enough, try a smaller vessel. Do not shout. The pot's note is about the pitch of a child's or woman's voice, so a child often finds it, while a deep adult voice may slide past it. The boom is soft, so keep the room quiet and listen with the pot close. Typical, not promised: the effect is clearer with a deep pot than a shallow one. Measure the depth with the ruler and write it down.
flow.context: In this step, you find the hidden note of the big pot.

flow.do: Do the same with the small vessel. Compare which one boomed at a lower note. Then try the bathroom, with the door shut. Hum a slow slide from low to high and listen for a note that suddenly seems bigger.
flow.say: Now try the small tumbler. Is its hidden note lower or higher? Then go into the bathroom and shut the door. Hum slowly from low to high. Is there a note where the room seems to boom?
flow.kid: Try the small vessel. Is the note higher? Then try the bathroom.
flow.parent: Expected: the small vessel answers at a higher note than the big one. The small bathroom often has a note where a hum sounds big, and this is why singing in the bathroom sounds good. A bathroom's note is very low, so a deep adult voice finds it more easily, and a child may find none. Let a deep-voiced adult try if there is one. In a group, one person hums and the others listen from the doorway to say if it sounded bigger. Compare depth too: the deeper vessel should answer at the lower note. If nothing booms, that is a real result.

check.q: The small tumbler booms at a higher note than the big pot. What is the best reason?
options: The smaller space has a shorter air column, so its natural note is higher
The tumbler is lighter
The tumbler is made of a different metal
check.why: A smaller space has a shorter air column and a higher natural note, just like a shorter pipe. Weight and metal matter much less. A child who picks 'lighter' is thinking of a falling thing, not of the air inside.

flow.context: In this step, you compare vessels and try the bathroom.

flow.do: Ask your child for their claim, evidence and reasoning. Then ask where else they have heard a space answer back, such as a stairwell, a temple hall or a well.
flow.say: What is your claim about which space answers at the lowest note? What did you notice? Why do you think so? Where else have you heard a place answer back when you sing or shout?
flow.kid: Which space gave the lowest note? Why? Where else have you heard this?

ask.q: Why does singing in a bathroom sound better than singing in a field?
good: The walls bounce the sound back.
The room boosts some notes.
The space answers at some notes and makes them louder.

flow.context: In this step, you say what you found and link it to places you know.

projects.title: The Bottle Bansuri Set: tune five bottles to play a scale

materials.item: 5 identical glass bottles with narrow necks, each holding about 250 to 300 millilitres, small soda or juice bottles
a measuring cup with millilitre marks
water, and a small jug
a harmonium, a keyboard, or a free keyboard app on a phone, to give the notes Sa, Re, Ga, Pa and Dha
tape (any tape or paper strips) and a marker, to label the bottles
a folded towel to stand the bottles on

projects.safety: Use glass bottles without chips or cracks, and stand them on a towel. Rest between rounds of blowing, and stop if anyone feels dizzy. Each child blows into their own bottle, or wipes the mouth with a clean cloth before the next child blows. Pick a quiet time, since five bottles can be loud.

schedule.what: Tune the five bottles to Sa, Re, Ga, Pa and Dha by adding water, and label them.
Practise a short tune, play it for the family, and record the water amounts in a table.

projects.record: A table with five bottles, the note names, the amount of water in each and the air column length. A note on whether equal steps in notes need equal steps in water.
projects.context: In this project, you tune five bottles to a scale by changing the water in each, and then play a tune on them by blowing across the tops.

setup.art: Five bottles in a row with different amounts of water, labelled Sa, Re, Ga, Pa and Dha.
setup.caption: 1. Label five bottles Sa, Re, Ga, Pa and Dha.

setup.art: A child blowing across one bottle while a parent plays the matching note on a harmonium.
setup.caption: 2. Blow across a bottle, and match its note to the harmonium by adding or pouring out water.

setup.art: A family in a row, one blowing across the bottles while others listen and clap.
setup.caption: 3. Play a tune and perform it for the family.

flow.do: Show your child the bottles and the harmonium or keyboard. Ask for a guess and a reason about which bottle will need the most water for Sa and which for Dha.
flow.say: We will tune five bottles to Sa, Re, Ga, Pa and Dha, by changing the water. Which note needs the most water, Sa or Dha? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tune five bottles to a scale with water. Which needs most water, Sa or Dha?

ask.q: Why do you think that note needs more water?
good: More water means a shorter air column and a higher note.
A low note needs lots of air, so little water.
I will have to try it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The answer is that Dha, the highest, needs the most water, because the air column is shortest. Children may need the Tap or Blow test first to remember this. Roles: with one child, you play the keyboard note and your child tunes the bottle. With 2 to 4 children, each child tunes one or two bottles, then all come together to play the tune, one bottle each.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle Bansuri Set. You guess before you build.

flow.do: First blow across the empty bottle and find its note on the harmonium or keyboard. Call that note Sa. Now play Re, Ga, Pa and Dha above it. For each next bottle, start with the first-guess amount in the parent note and blow across it. If the note is too low, add water. If it is too high, pour a little out. Match it, and label the bottle. Each bottle needs more water than the one before.
flow.say: Play Sa on the harmonium. Blow across the first bottle and compare. Is yours lower or higher? Add water to go higher, or pour some out to go lower. Match it, and label it. Then do Re, Ga, Pa and Dha.
flow.kid: Play a note. Blow across a bottle. Add water to go higher. Pour out to go lower.
flow.parent: A bottle's lowest blown note is often below the harmonium's usual Sa, so we start from the bottle's own note, and the empty bottle is Sa. Typical first guesses for a 250 to 300 millilitre bottle, to be tuned by ear: Re about 50 millilitres, Ga about 90, Pa about 140, Dha about 170. Your bottles will differ, so trust your ears. Add water in small amounts, 10 millilitres at a time. Blow gently, because a hard blow jumps to a higher note. The water goes up and up as you climb the scale. If you have no harmonium, use a keyboard app on a phone, or sing the scale and match by ear. Write the amounts of water as you go.

check.q: A bottle is blown across and its note is too high. What should you do to lower it?
options: Pour a little water out, to make the air column longer
Add more water
Put on a lid
check.why: A longer air column gives a lower note. Pouring water out makes the air column longer. Adding water would make the note even higher. A lid would stop the sound altogether.

flow.context: In this step, you tune the five bottles.

flow.do: On day 2, check that each bottle still gives the right note, since water may have evaporated or been spilled. Fix any that are off. Practise playing Sa, Re, Ga, Pa, Dha and back.
flow.say: Check each bottle against the harmonium again. Add or remove a little water if one is off. Then play the scale up and down.
flow.kid: Check each bottle. Fix any that are off. Play the scale.
flow.parent: Water in a bottle can evaporate a little overnight, and in hot weather a bit more. Cover the bottles with a plate if you want to keep them. If you need to start again, you only lose ten minutes. The note changes only a little, but it can be heard. Write down any water you had to add.
flow.context: In this step, you check the tuning on day 2 and practise.

flow.do: Choose a short tune made of those five notes. Practise it, and then play it for the family. Write down the water amounts and the air column lengths in your table. Notice if equal steps in notes needed equal steps in water.
flow.say: Choose a tune that uses only these five notes. Practise it a few times, and then play it for the family. Afterwards, look at your table. Did each step up the scale need the same extra water?
flow.kid: Pick a tune. Practise it. Play it for your family. Look at your water amounts.

ask.q: Did each step up the scale need the same extra water?
good: No, the higher steps needed more water.
Some steps needed a lot more than others.
The water amounts were not even.

flow.parent: Expected: the amounts of water do not rise evenly. Notes are spaced by ratios, not by equal steps, and a bottle's note depends on its air volume in a more complicated way than a plain pipe. Do not worry if your numbers look uneven. Typical, not promised: going from Sa to Dha, the air in the bottle shrinks to roughly a third. If you have only a few bottles, play a three-note tune (Sa, Ga, Pa).
flow.context: In this step, you play a tune for the family and study your table.

challenges.title: One Tube, Three Notes
challenges.problem: You have one cardboard tube, such as a kitchen foil roll tube. Make it play three clearly different notes without making it any longer. Then play three notes in a row, each held for two seconds.
constraints: Use only one cardboard tube, about 25 to 30 centimetres long. You may use tape, clay and paper.
A grown-up does all the cutting. Cut off no more than a third of the tube, and keep every piece.
The notes must be made only by blowing across the tube. No humming into it, and no buzzing of the lips.
The three notes must be clearly different, so that a listener with their eyes closed can tell them apart.
Hold each note steady for two seconds.
materials: a cardboard tube from a roll of kitchen foil or cling film, about 4 centimetres across
a little modelling clay or a ball of paper
a pair of scissors, used by a grown-up
a paper strip or a little tape, to narrow the opening if the tube will not sing
general: Cover the far end of the tube with your palm for a lower note, and uncover it for a higher note. A tube closed at one end sounds an octave lower than the same tube open at both ends.
Stop the far end with a plug of clay, and slide a second piece of tube in to shorten the air column.
Cut the tube shorter in steps and use three different lengths.
creative: Make two small holes in the side, covered with tape, like a bansuri. Uncover them one at a time to shorten the air column.
Slide one tube inside another, like a trombone, to change the length as you play.
Use a funnel of paper at the end to make the note louder, and tune it by pushing the paper in.
Fill part of the tube with water to shorten the air column, using a tube that is closed at the bottom.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design on paper. Build it and test it. Change one thing, such as the position of a hole, and test again. Which design gave the three clearest notes? Why do you think it worked?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about air columns. You change the length of the air inside a tube to change the note.

setup.art: A child with a cardboard tube held to her lips, blowing across the open end, with sound lines rising.
setup.caption: 1. Blow across the open end of the tube and find a note.

setup.art: The same child with her palm covering the far end of the tube, and a lower note drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the far end with your palm. The note goes lower.

setup.art: A tube with two taped holes on its side, one finger lifting the tape from the first hole.
setup.caption: 3. Try side holes covered with tape, and uncover them one at a time.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three ways to change the air column in the tube.
flow.say: You have one tube, and you must get three notes out of it. What changes the note of an air column? Draw some ideas for how you could make the air column longer or shorter.
flow.kid: One tube. Three notes. Draw two ideas for changing the air.

ask.q: What changes the note of a tube?
good: The length of the air column.
Whether the far end is open or closed.
How hard I blow.

flow.context: This is the first step of the One Tube, Three Notes challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Learn to get a note first. Hold the tube upright and rest your lower lip on one edge of the open end. Blow a thin stream across the opening. Find the position that gives a clear note. Then cover the far end with your palm and listen again.
flow.say: Rest your lower lip on the edge of the tube. Blow a thin stream across the opening. When it sings, hold the tube still. Now cover the far end with your palm and blow again. What changes?
flow.kid: Blow across the end of the tube. Find a note. Cover the far end. What changes?
flow.parent: It takes time to find the sweet spot. Tilt the tube a little. If it still will not sing, wet your lower lip. Expected: with the far end closed, the note is about an octave lower. If your child cannot make a note, use a shorter tube first, or tape a thin paper strip over half of the opening, so the air has a sharp edge to hit. A wide tube is harder to sing than a narrow one, so a thinner tube or a plastic bottle neck also works. In a group, each child needs their own tube and a turn at the cutting-helper role, never at the scissors.

check.q: Covering the far end of the tube makes the note lower. What is the best reason?
options: A tube closed at one end has a natural note about an octave lower than the same tube open at both ends
The palm adds weight
The palm makes the sound softer
check.why: A tube with both ends open vibrates twice as fast as the same tube closed at one end, so closing it gives a note an octave lower. It is about the air column, not the weight of the palm.

flow.context: In this step, you learn to get a note and try covering the end.

flow.do: Build your first design. Test whether it gives three clearly different notes. Ask a listener with their eyes closed to tell the notes apart. Write down what works.
flow.say: Build your first design. Play your three notes. Ask a listener with their eyes closed whether they can tell them apart. Write down what worked and what did not.
flow.kid: Build your design. Play three notes. Can a listener tell them apart?
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts any holes with scissors, with the child watching from a distance, and keeps all the pieces. With 2 to 4 children, each child designs and tests their own tube, then the group votes which tube gave the clearest notes. Mark the hole positions with a pencil first. Tell the child that holes nearer the far end change the note less than holes near the blowing end. The first try rarely works, and that is fine.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test your first design.

flow.do: Change one thing in your design. Test again. Then try to play three notes in a row, each held for two seconds. Time them.
flow.say: Change one thing, such as the position of a hole or the length of the tube. Test again. Then play three notes in a row, two seconds each. Count slowly in your head.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Play three notes, two seconds each.

ask.q: What did you change, and what did it do to the note?
good: I moved the hole closer to my mouth and the note went higher.
A shorter air column gave a higher note.
Closing the end gave a lower note.

flow.context: In this step, you improve your design and play three notes in a row.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain which design worked best, and how it uses the length of the air column.
flow.say: Which design gave the three clearest notes? How did you change the air column? How is a bansuri like your tube?
flow.kid: Which design was best? How did you change the air?

ask.q: How is a bansuri like your tube?
good: Both have holes to shorten the air column.
Both make the note by blowing across an edge.
A bansuri is a tube with holes in the side.

flow.context: In this step, you link your tube to a bansuri.

worksheets.title: Four Ways to Start a Sound (core)

items.p: A balloon bursting makes a bang. Which way of starting a sound is this?
items.why: A burst balloon gives the air one sudden push. There is no steady vibration, so it is a pop. Choosing 'solid shaking' pictures the balloon skin vibrating like a drum, but it breaks in one snap.

items.p: One vibration each second is called one ____.
items.why: The hertz is the unit for counting vibrations. A note of 440 hertz vibrates 440 times each second.

items.p: A string that is half as long vibrates twice as fast and gives a note one octave higher. True or false?
items.why: True. Halving the length doubles the number of vibrations each second, which is one octave. This rule works for strings and for air columns.

items.p: A bansuri gives its lowest note when all its holes are covered. What is the best reason?
opts: The air column is at its longest
The air column is at its shortest
items.why: Covering the holes makes the whole length of the tube vibrate, which is the longest air column and the lowest note. Uncovering holes shortens the air column and raises the note.

items.p: Blow across three bottles: one empty, one with 200 millilitres of water and one with 400 millilitres. Put them in order from the lowest note to the highest.
items.why: More water leaves less air, and a shorter air column gives a higher note when you blow. So the empty bottle is lowest and the fullest is highest.
items.art: Three identical bottles in a row with different water levels, and empty circles above them to number from lowest to highest.

items.p: Match each sound to the way it is started.
items.why: A string is a shaking solid. A bansuri works by air shaking in its tube. Thunder is a shock wave from lightning. Chalk grips and slips along the board.

items.p: You tap a glass bottle and the one with the most water gives the lowest note. What is shaking?
opts: Only the air above the water
items.why: When you tap a bottle, the glass wall and the water inside shake. More water is more to shake, so the note is lower. When you blow across, it is the air that shakes, and the order flips.

items.p: The mix of overtones in a sound gives it its ____, so a flute and a violin sound different on the same note.
items.why: Timbre is the quality of a sound. It depends on which overtones are strong and which are weak.

items.p: A damp finger squeaks on glass, but a dry finger hardly does. What is the best reason?
opts: A squeak needs the finger to stick and slip again and again, and a dry finger grips too hard to do that
A dry finger makes no vibration at all
The glass is warmer when damp
items.why: A squeak is a fast rhythm of gripping and slipping. If the grip is too strong, the finger drags. If it is too weak, the finger glides. Damp is in the middle.

items.p: When you whisper, your vocal folds buzz very quietly. True or false?
items.why: False. In a whisper, the vocal folds do not buzz. Air rushes through a gap in the throat and makes a hiss. You can feel the difference by touching your throat.

items.p: Which parts of the body shape the buzz from the vocal folds into the vowels 'ee' and 'oo'?
items.why: The throat, mouth and nose form a space that boosts some overtones of the buzz more than others. Changing the shape of the space changes the vowel.

items.p: Sort these sounds into the four ways a sound can start.
items.why: Skins and bells are shaking solids. Bottles and whistles work by air shaking in a space. A clap and a balloon are one sudden push. A hinge and a cricket rub two surfaces that stick and slip.

items.p: How can you find how far away lightning is?
opts: Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, and divide by three to get kilometres
Count the flashes in a minute
Listen for how loud the thunder is
Measure how bright the flash is
items.why: Light arrives almost at once, and sound travels about a kilometre in three seconds. So the gap in seconds divided by three is the distance in kilometres.

items.p: A friend says that every sound is a steady note. Give two sounds that are not steady notes, and say why.
items.a: A clap and a hiss are not steady notes. A clap is one sudden push of air, and a hiss is a jumble of many pitches with no steady one.
items.why: A strong answer names two sounds, such as a clap, a pop, a hiss or a crash, and says that they have no single steady pitch.

items.p: Explain to a younger child why blowing across a bottle with more water gives a higher note.
items.a: When you blow across a bottle, the air inside shakes. More water leaves less air, so the air column is shorter. A shorter air column shakes faster, and that gives a higher note.
items.why: A strong answer says that the air is what shakes, that more water means a shorter air column, and that a shorter column is a higher note.

items.p: Draw two bottles, one with a lot of water and one with a little. Mark the air column in each, and say which gives the higher note when blown across.
items.a: A bottle with a lot of water has a short air column marked at the top and gives the higher note. A bottle with a little water has a long air column and gives the lower note.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the air column as the empty part of each bottle, shorter in the fuller one, and gives the higher note to the fuller bottle.
items.art: Two empty bottle outlines side by side, with space to draw different water levels.

items.p: A closed pipe 17 centimetres long gives about 500 hertz. About what note does a closed pipe 34 centimetres long give?
items.why: Doubling the length halves the number of vibrations each second. 500 divided by 2 is 250. That is one octave lower.

items.p: A string vibrates 200 times each second. You press it at its middle so only half can shake. What happens?
opts: It vibrates about 400 times each second, one octave higher
It vibrates about 100 times each second
items.why: Half the length means twice the vibrations each second. 200 times 2 is 400. Picking 100 reverses the rule.

items.p: A string two thirds as long as another vibrates one and a half times as fast and gives the note Pa above Sa. So Sa and Pa have a ratio of 3 to ____.
items.why: One and a half is the same as 3 over 2. Sa and Pa have a ratio of 3 to 2, which is what makes them agree.

items.p: A hollow bamboo pole that moans in the wind is vibrating like a stretched string. True or false?
items.why: False. The air in the hollow pole is what shakes. The wind flips from side to side at the edge of the opening, and the air inside picks the note. The bamboo itself hardly moves.

items.p: Why can a flute player move the note up by blowing harder?
opts: The edge tone speeds up and jumps to a higher resonance of the air column
Blowing harder makes the flute shorter
items.why: Faster air makes faster swirls at the edge, and the edge tone locks on to a higher resonance of the air column. The flute itself does not change.

items.p: Why does a thin wire hum at a higher note in the wind than a thick wire?
opts: The swirls behind a thin wire flip from side to side more often
The wind blows harder on thin wires
items.why: The rate of the flips grows as the wire gets thinner. The thin wire gives faster swirls, so a higher hum. Weight and temperature are not the cause.

items.p: Sort each description into 'fundamental' or 'overtone'.
items: a string swinging as one big loop
a string swinging in two halves at once
the lowest and usually strongest vibration
a higher vibration that sounds along with the main note
the part that sets the pitch you hear
the part that shapes the timbre
items.why: The fundamental is the slowest vibration and sets the pitch. Overtones are faster vibrations above it, and the mix of them gives the sound its timbre.

items.p: Put these in order from the one whose air gives the highest natural note to the lowest: a big clay jar, a small tin cup, a steel pot.
items.why: A smaller space has a shorter air column and a higher natural note. The tin cup is smallest, then the steel pot, then the big clay jar.
items.art: A small tin cup, a steel pot and a tall clay jar side by side.

items.p: Match each action to what is shaking.
pairs: Drawing a bow across a violin string
The string, driven by stick and slip
items.why: Different actions make different things shake. Knowing what shakes explains the note.

items.p: Why does thunder arrive after you see the lightning?
opts: Sound travels much more slowly than light
items.why: Lightning and thunder start together. Light reaches you almost at once, and sound travels about a kilometre in three seconds.

items.p: A mosquito's wings beat about 500 times each second and a bee's about 230. Which whines higher, and why?
opts: The mosquito, because her wings vibrate faster
The bee, because she is bigger
The bee, because her wings are slower
items.why: A faster vibration gives a higher pitch. 500 is more than twice 230, so the mosquito is more than an octave higher.

items.p: Whispered 'ee' and 'oo' can be told apart because the vocal folds buzz in different ways. True or false?
items.why: False. The vocal folds do not buzz in a whisper. The mouth takes a different shape for each vowel, and the shape boosts different parts of the hiss.

items.p: Why do some pairs of notes sound sweet together? People who have thought about it give different answers.

views.who: A follower of Pythagoras in ancient Greece
views.says: Notes sound sweet when their string lengths are in simple ratios like 2 to 1 and 3 to 2. The world is built on numbers, and the sweetness is a sign of this.

views.who: Hermann von Helmholtz, a German scientist
views.says: Notes close together make beats, a fast wobble that sounds rough. Notes sound sweet when their overtones do not beat. The ear is the judge.

views.who: Josh McDermott, a scientist in the USA
views.says: People who live far from Western music did not prefer sweet pairs to rough ones. A lot of what sounds sweet may be learned from the music around us.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing, and what would you test to check it?
items.a: Any view is fine if the reason uses evidence, such as ratios, beats or the results with the Tsimane people.
items.why: No one has settled this question. A strong answer names a view, gives a reason, and says what test would help, such as playing the same pairs to people who grew up with different music.

items.p: Label the three parts of the voice on the drawing of a head: 'vocal folds buzz', 'mouth shapes the vowel' and 'air comes from the lungs'.
a: chest: air comes from the lungs
items.why: Air from the lungs pushes the vocal folds, which buzz. The buzz passes through the throat and mouth, which shape it into vowels.
items.art: A side view of a head and chest, with three arrows pointing to the chest, the throat and the mouth, and empty boxes for labels.

items.p: Draw a string vibrating as one whole loop, and the same string vibrating in two halves. Mark which one gives the higher note.
items.a: The first string has one loop between its ends. The second has two loops, with a still point in the middle. The two-loop string is the higher note, one octave above.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one loop for the fundamental and two loops for the first overtone, and says that two loops vibrate twice as fast.
items.art: Two empty strings stretched between two points, with space to draw the shape of the vibration.

items.p: A friend says that a violin and a bansuri playing the same note should sound exactly the same. Write a reply.
items.a: They have the same pitch, but their timbre is different. A violin has many strong overtones from a stick-slip bow on a string, and a bansuri has a smoother mix from air shaking in a tube.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pitch is the same but the mix of overtones is different, and mentions that the sound is made in different ways.

items.p: A squeaky door goes quiet after a drop of oil. Explain what the oil did, using the words stick and slip.
items.a: The oil made the surfaces slide smoothly, so they no longer stick. Without sticking and slipping again and again, there is no fast vibration, and the squeak stops.
items.why: A strong answer says that a squeak is a rhythm of sticking and slipping and that oil removes the sticking.

items.p: A closed pipe gives a note of about 343 divided by four times its length in metres. About what note does a closed pipe 0.25 metres long give?
items.why: Four times 0.25 is 1. 343 divided by 1 is 343. Picking 86 forgets to divide by four times the length.

items.p: A closed pipe gives 300 hertz. Its length is cut in half. About what note does it give now?
items.why: Halving the length doubles the vibrations each second. 300 times 2 is 600, one octave higher.

items.p: Marin Mersenne found that a string vibrates faster when it is shorter, tighter or ____.
items.why: A thin string has less mass to move, so it vibrates faster. A thick string vibrates more slowly.

items.p: Cupped hands make a lower, hollow clap than flat hands because the cupped space picks out a pitch. True or false?
items.why: True. The air trapped in cupped hands acts like a small resonator, so the pop has a pitch. Flat hands give a sharper, higher clap.

items.p: You see a lightning flash, and thunder follows 9 seconds later. About how far away was the lightning?
items.why: Sound travels about a kilometre in three seconds. 9 divided by 3 is 3 kilometres.

items.p: A finger takes half a second to cross a window and squeaks at 800 hertz. About how many sticks and slips happen in that sweep?
items.why: 800 vibrations each second for half a second is 800 times a half, which is 400. Picking 800 forgets that the sweep only lasted half a second.

items.p: A grown-up man's voice buzz is about 110 hertz. In 2 seconds, his vocal folds open and close about ____ times.
items.why: 110 vibrations each second times 2 seconds is 220.

items.p: Match each thing to the idea that explains it.
pairs: Tanpura strings tuned to Pa and Sa
Notes that agree, with a simple ratio of 3 to 2
A bottle that sings when blown across
An edge tone joined to an air column
Swirls flipping from side to side
items.why: Each sound has a cause that you can name. Naming it is a first step to testing it.

items.p: In 1971, John Coltman found that listeners could not tell flutes with walls of different materials apart. What does this suggest?
opts: The wall material matters much less than the shape of the air column
items.why: If listeners cannot tell the walls apart, then the material has little effect on the sound. The air column carries most of the sound. Some players still disagree.

items.p: People of the Tsimane in Bolivia did not prefer sweet pairs of notes to rough ones. What does this suggest?
opts: Part of what sounds sweet is learned from the music around us
Sweet notes are the same for all people
items.why: If sweetness were fully built into the ear, every group would show it. The result suggests that learning plays a part. It does not show that ratios do not exist.

items.p: Explain why a bottle gives opposite orders of notes when it is tapped and when it is blown across. Use the words 'shaking' and 'air column'.
items.a: When you tap the bottle, the glass and the water are shaking, and more water is more to shake, so the note is lower. When you blow across it, the air column is shaking, and more water makes the air column shorter, so the note is higher.
items.why: A strong answer says what is shaking in each case and links it to the direction of the change.

items.p: A person who pinches their nose while saying 'mama' sounds different because the nose is part of the space that shapes the voice. True or false?
items.why: True. The nose is part of the vocal tract. Blocking it changes the shape of the space, so the sound changes.

items.p: Does the material of a flute change its tone?

views.who: A flute player who uses a silver flute
views.says: I can hear the difference between silver and wood when I play. The silver one is brighter.

views.who: A physicist who tested flutes in 1971
views.says: I made flutes with walls of different materials and asked listeners to tell them apart. They could not. The shape of the air column matters most.
The material changes how the flute feels to play, and a player who feels comfortable plays better. That may change the tone without changing the walls' sound.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing, and how would you test it?
items.a: Any view is fine if the reason uses evidence. A good test would have the same player play several flutes behind a screen, with listeners who do not know which is which.
items.why: No one has settled this. A strong answer names a view and suggests a test that hides which flute is which, so that expectations do not change what people hear.

items.p: Draw the vocal tract as a bottle shape, and show where the buzz starts and where the vowel is made.
items.a: A bottle shape for the throat and mouth. A zig-zag buzz at the bottom where the vocal folds are, and the mouth shape at the top labelled as where the vowel is made.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the buzz starting at the vocal folds and the space above shaping it.

items.p: Label what is happening when a violin is played: 'bow sticks and slips', 'string shakes', 'body of the violin shakes' and 'air carries the sound'.
a: bow touching the string: bow sticks and slips
the wooden box: body of the violin shakes
the space around: air carries the sound
items.why: A violin uses more than one way at once. The bow sticks and slips on the string, the string shakes, the body shakes and pushes the air, and the air carries the sound to the ear.
items.art: A violin with a bow drawn across the strings, with four arrows pointing to the bow, the string, the body and the air around.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether a sticky finger or a smooth finger squeaks louder on glass. Say what you keep the same.
items.a: I would use the same glass, the same finger, the same press and the same speed. I would change only how sticky the finger is, and have a listener with eyes shut score each squeak. I would do each condition three times.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, uses repeated tries and avoids the listener knowing which finger it is.

quiz.p: A sound starts when something pushes on the air. Which of these does not push on the air?
opts: A stream of air across an edge
quiz.why: Something has to move to push the air. A stone lying still does nothing to the air. A string, a clap and a moving air stream all push it.
One hertz is one vibration each second. Loudness is a different idea.

quiz.p: Two strings are the same except that one is half as long. Compared with the long one, the short one vibrates...
quiz.why: Halving the length doubles the vibrations each second, which is one octave higher.

quiz.p: What does timbre tell you about a sound?
opts: Which instrument or voice is making it, even when the pitch is the same
quiz.why: Timbre is the quality of a sound, which comes from the mix of overtones. Loudness and distance are different ideas.

quiz.p: You touch a vibrating string lightly at its middle. What do you hear?
opts: A note one octave higher, with a pure bell-like sound
A louder sound at the same pitch
quiz.why: The touch stops the whole-string vibration and leaves the two-half vibration, which is one octave higher.

quiz.p: You blow across two identical bottles. One has 100 millilitres of water and the other has 300 millilitres. Which gives the higher note, and why?
opts: The 300 millilitre bottle, because its air column is shorter
The 100 millilitre bottle, because its air column is shorter
The 300 millilitre bottle, because the water is heavier
quiz.why: More water leaves less air, so the air column is shorter, and a shorter air column gives a higher note. Picking 'heavier' is the reasoning for tapping, not blowing.

quiz.p: What makes the note of a flute?
opts: Air in the tube, set shaking by a stream of air across an edge
The metal of the flute shaking
quiz.why: A flute is a tube of air. The air stream across the edge sets the air column shaking, and the length of the column picks the note.

quiz.p: Which of these makes a sound from one sudden push of air, with no steady pitch?
quiz.why: A clap is one sudden squeeze of air. The other three give steady notes.

quiz.p: A squeak happens when two surfaces...
opts: stick and slip again and again
slide with no grip at all
quiz.why: A squeak is a very fast rhythm of gripping and slipping. If there is no grip, or too much, there is no squeak.

quiz.p: In a whisper, what turns the hiss into 'ee' or 'oo'?
opts: The buzz of the vocal folds
quiz.why: A whisper has no buzz. The mouth shape boosts different parts of the hiss for each vowel.

quiz.p: Which statement about vocal folds is true?
opts: They buzz when you speak or hum, and do not buzz when you whisper
They only buzz when you shout
quiz.why: The vocal folds buzz for speech, singing and humming. In a whisper, air only hisses through a gap.

quiz.p: Which of these is still an open question for scientists?
opts: Why some pairs of notes sound sweet to nearly everyone
Whether a clap is louder than a whisper
quiz.why: Scientists agree that vibrations make sound. Why certain pairs of notes feel sweet is still debated, with ideas from physics, the ear and learning.

applications: Tuning musical instruments with a tuner that reads the hertz of a note, so that a tanpura, a guitar or a piano is in tune.
Making flutes, bansuris and organ pipes, where the length of the air column and the places of the holes decide the notes.
Designing silencers for scooters and cars, which cut down the pops and bangs of the engine.
Building halls, studios and auditoriums, where scientists check which notes the room boosts, so that speech and music sound clear.
Speech recognition and teaching of speech, which use the shapes of the vowels to tell sounds apart.
Designing tall chimneys, bridges and cables so that wind swirls do not make them hum or shake.
Stopping the squeal of brakes and the squeak of hinges, by changing the grip between surfaces.
Making whistles, sirens and alarms that can be heard from far away.
Using rosin on violin bows and chalk on climbing hands, which change how surfaces stick and slip.
Using the hum and echo of a pipe or a tank to check its size and whether it is full.

open_questions.q: Why do some pairs of notes sound sweet to nearly everyone?
open_questions.why_open: Ideas from ratios, from the ear and from learning all have some evidence. No one idea explains it all.

open_questions.q: Where does the flash of light come from when a snapping shrimp's bubble collapses?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists found the flash in 2001. The bubble is tiny and lasts a tiny moment, and they are still working out the details.

open_questions.q: How exactly do the biggest whales make their very deep songs?
open_questions.why_open: Whales sing without opening their mouths, and their bodies are hard to study alive. Scientists are still working out how the sound is made.

open_questions.q: Can a person who has never heard any music still find some sounds sweet?
open_questions.why_open: It is hard to find people who have never heard music, so the question is hard to test fairly.

open_questions.q: How does the brain turn a mix of overtones into the single sense of one note?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the ear splits sound into pitches, but how the brain joins them back into one note is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How many different sounds can one human voice make?
open_questions.why_open: People keep inventing new sounds, from throat singing to beatboxing. No one has counted, and perhaps no one can.

maths.problem: A note of 440 hertz sounds for 5 seconds. How many vibrations is that? A honeybee's wings beat 230 times each second. How many beats in the same 5 seconds?
maths.answer: 2200 vibrations for the note, and 1150 wingbeats for the bee.
maths.explain: Each second has 440 vibrations. 440 times 5 is 2200. The bee beats 230 times each second. 230 times 5 is 1150.
maths.context: Hertz counts vibrations each second, so a longer sound holds more vibrations.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a rate by a time tells you how many vibrations there were, which is how scientists first counted sounds.

maths.problem: A singer's Sa is 130 hertz. The upper Sa is one octave higher, so it vibrates twice as fast. What is the upper Sa? What would a note two octaves above the first Sa be?
maths.answer: The upper Sa is 260 hertz. Two octaves above is 520 hertz.
maths.explain: One octave doubles the number: 130 times 2 is 260. Another octave doubles it again: 260 times 2 is 520. Two octaves is 4 times the first note.
maths.context: An octave doubles the vibrations each second, so a row of octaves is a doubling pattern.
maths.why_maths: Noticing the doubling pattern lets you find any octave without having to measure it.

maths.problem: An empty bottle has an air column of 24 centimetres. Each 100 millilitres of water takes 4 centimetres off the air column. How long is the air column with 100, 200 and 300 millilitres? How many times shorter is the air column with 300 millilitres than the empty one? What do you expect the note to do?
maths.answer: 20, 16 and 12 centimetres. The 300 millilitre air column is half as long. The note should rise, perhaps by about an octave for a plain pipe.
maths.explain: 24 take away 4 is 20, then 16, then 12. 24 divided by 12 is 2, so the column is half as long. A shorter air column gives a higher note, and half the length is about one octave.
maths.context: In the Tap or Blow test, you pour water into bottles and shorten the air column.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one length by another shows how many times shorter the air column is, which predicts how much the note will rise.

maths.problem: A singer's Sa is 240 hertz. Pa vibrates three halves as fast as Sa. How many hertz is Pa? The upper Sa is twice Sa. How many hertz is that? Which is bigger, the step from Sa to Pa or the step from Pa to upper Sa?
maths.answer: Pa is 360 hertz. The upper Sa is 480 hertz. The step from Sa to Pa is 120 hertz, and from Pa to upper Sa is 120 hertz too, but in ratio they are different.
maths.explain: Half of 240 is 120, and 240 plus 120 is 360. Twice 240 is 480. 360 minus 240 is 120 and 480 minus 360 is 120. The steps are equal in hertz. But 360 to 240 is a ratio of 3 to 2, and 480 to 360 is a ratio of 4 to 3, so the ear hears them as different.
maths.context: Sa and Pa have a ratio of 3 to 2, and the upper Sa is twice Sa.
maths.why_maths: Finding a fraction of a number gives the hertz for each note, and shows that equal gaps in hertz are not equal gaps in sound.

maths.problem: You see lightning, and count 12 seconds before the thunder. Sound travels about a kilometre in 3 seconds. How far away was the lightning? If it was only 1 kilometre away, how many seconds would you count?
maths.answer: 4 kilometres. For 1 kilometre you would count 3 seconds.
maths.explain: 12 divided by 3 is 4. For 1 kilometre, 1 times 3 is 3 seconds.
maths.context: Thunder is a shock wave from lightning, and it travels slower than light.
maths.why_maths: Dividing seconds by three turns a count into a distance, so you can tell whether a storm is coming closer.

maths.problem: A finger takes half a second to cross 30 centimetres of window and squeaks at 800 hertz. How many sticks and slips happen in the sweep? How far does the finger move in each one?
maths.answer: 400 sticks and slips. Each moves the finger 0.075 centimetres, which is less than 1 millimetre.
maths.explain: 800 times a half is 400. The finger travels 30 centimetres in 400 steps. 30 divided by 400 is 0.075 centimetres. There are 10 millimetres in a centimetre, so that is 0.75 millimetres.
maths.context: In the Squeak Test, a damp finger sticks and slips many times as it moves across glass.
maths.why_maths: Splitting a distance among many steps shows how tiny each stick and slip is, which you could never see by eye.

maths.problem: In a Whisper Vowels test, a listener got 24 out of 30 whispered vowels right. With three vowels to choose from, guessing alone would give about 10 out of 30. How many more than guessing is that? What share of 30 was right?
maths.answer: 14 more than guessing. 24 out of 30 is 8 out of every 10, or 80 out of every 100.
maths.explain: 24 minus 10 is 14. 24 out of 30 is the same as 8 out of 10, because dividing both by 3 gives 8 and 10. That is 80 out of every 100.
maths.context: In the Whisper Vowels activity, a listener tries to tell three vowels apart in a whisper.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a score with the score that guessing would give tells you whether the listener really heard a difference.

maths.problem: A closed pipe gives a note of about 343 divided by four times its length in metres. What note does a closed tube 25 centimetres long give? What note does a closed tube 50 centimetres long give?
maths.answer: About 343 hertz for the 25 centimetre tube, and about 172 hertz for the 50 centimetre tube.
maths.explain: 25 centimetres is 0.25 metres. Four times 0.25 is 1. 343 divided by 1 is 343. 50 centimetres is 0.5 metres. Four times 0.5 is 2. 343 divided by 2 is 171.5, which is about 172. Doubling the length halves the note.
maths.context: In the One Tube, Three Notes challenge, you change the air column of a tube to change its note.
maths.why_maths: A rule with numbers lets you choose a tube length to match the note you want.

founder: Founder's notebook, Sound: the concept activities on Sound and Vibration and on Waves and Oscillation. Used ideas include tapping glasses with different water levels, straw panpipes, rubbing a glass rim for a tone, and the Chladni plate with sand, which became the bottle test, the squeak test and the section on plates.

The Class 3 unit on where sounds come from, which this unit builds on. It showed that every sound starts with a vibration. This unit asks how many different ways the air can be pushed, and what shapes the note.
The founder's idea that a sound belongs to its source and to the space around it, used for the deep truth and the Roots card.
science: Marin Mersenne, Harmonie universelle, 1636 (laws for vibrating strings, overtones, and the speed of sound for all pitches)
Galileo Galilei, Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Concerning Two New Sciences, 1638 (lines scraped by a chisel and the idea that pitch is the number of vibrations)
Ernst Chladni, Entdeckungen ueber die Theorie des Klanges, 1787 (sand patterns on plates), and the Paris Academy prize won by Sophie Germain in 1816
Joseph Fourier, Theorie analytique de la chaleur, 1822, and Hermann von Helmholtz, On the Sensations of Tone, 1863 (timbre and resonators)
Vincenc Strouhal, 'Ueber eine besondere Art der Tonerregung', 1878 (singing wires)
C. V. Raman, 'On some Indian stringed instruments', Proceedings of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, 1921 (the tanpura and veena)
Gunnar Fant, Acoustic Theory of Speech Production, 1960 (source and filter)
John W. Coltman, 'Effect of material on flute tone quality', Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1971

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Tap or Blow: five identical narrow-necked glass bottles and a folded towel are enough. Blowing across a bottle takes a minute or two to learn, so the steps give a tip, say to rest, and say that plastic bottles work for blowing but not for tapping. The reversal is clear in glass bottles, and the steps say what to write if it is not. Squeak Test: use a clean window pane at ground level, or a mirror. Damp fingers squeak best, wet and dry ones barely do, and oily ones are silent. The steps say to wipe the glass between tries and to clean oil off the floor. Whisper Vowels: a cardboard screen stops lip-reading, and the slips go back each time so the test is fair. Most listeners get 8 or more out of 10 whispered vowels right. The Pot That Hums Back: a deep voice finds the big pot's note more easily, and the steps say what to do if nothing booms. Bottle Bansuri Set: a harmonium, a toy keyboard or a keyboard app gives the notes, and the steps say to add water in small amounts. One Tube, Three Notes: a grown-up does all the cutting. Stay away from firecrackers and never pop anything close to an ear. Facts to verify before release: Archytas and the belief that high notes travel faster; Mersenne's finding that sound speed does not depend on pitch; the Coltman 1971 result; the 1816 Germain prize details; Raman's 1921 work on the tanpura; the Tsimane study; the typical pitches of voices and wings, which are rounded; and the speeds of sound used in the pipe rule. Numbers that are not certain are marked 'about' or 'reported'. The videos are still to be chosen.
